articles.title: Mohamed L'Ghacham and the Borrowed Family Album
articles.summary: A muralist from Tangier asks people for their old photographs, then paints them across the walls of the towns they came from.
articles.description: How Mohamed L'Ghacham, born in Tangier in 1993 and based near Barcelona, paints family snapshots and archive photographs as murals, from Casa Paquita in Mallorca to Vienna.
articles.body:
In October 2017, on one of the oldest houses in Can Picafort, on the north coast of Mallorca, Mohamed L'Ghacham painted a group of children. They were the children of the woman who owned the house, Paquita, as they had looked about forty years earlier, standing in the same place. The picture came from her family photographs, and she let him use it. The mural, made for the Saladina Art Fest, is called Casa Paquita.

That arrangement, a stranger's snapshot returned to the street where it was taken, sits at the centre of his work.

A painter from Tangier

L'Ghacham was born in Tangier, Morocco, in 1993 and is based in Mataró, on the coast north of Barcelona. He found graffiti at school, and only later the classical painters. His first murals, he told Colossal in 2021, were painted in abandoned or demolished places, or on the outskirts of cities.

Borrowed pictures

Festival organisers describe his painting as figurative and close to realism, with Impressionist touches, drawn from photographs of the late twentieth century. Colossal, writing in 2019, noticed what he paints: meals, table settings, toasts, people gathered together. It also noticed that he prefers photographs with small accidents in them, because they make the scene feel real.

The pictures increasingly come from the places he paints. By 2021 he was working from snapshots and home videos lent by neighbours, and from city archives. In Estarreja, Portugal, he painted the doctor Egas Moniz with his assistant Deolinda, from a 1930s photograph taken at Santa Marta Hospital in Lisbon and kept in Moniz's archive.

What the pictures say

Some walls carry a point of view. In Ostend he painted a woman cutting a birthday cake. The city's art route says he wanted to show the mother as an important member of the family, and saw the cake as a sign of how things get divided unequally. That painting can no longer be seen.

In Vienna, for Calle Libre's 2025 walls, he painted a family at a meal while plants grow over the scene. The festival describes it as almost a fading memory, and as a small utopia within reach.

Walls that do not last

Murals are exposed to weather, building work and new paint, and the Ostend wall shows how quickly one can go. Our reading is that the short life suits the material. A picture kept for decades in a drawer spends a few years where the whole street can see it.

articles.title: Rene Matić and the People in the Pictures
articles.summary: A London photographer turned pictures of friends and family into a Turner Prize nomination and, a year later, a major photography prize.
articles.description: How Rene Matić, born in Peterborough in 1997, built a practice from photographs of family, friends and community, from Central Saint Martins to the Turner Prize 2025 shortlist and the 2026 Deutsche Börse Photography Foundation Prize.
articles.body:
Most photographers point the camera outwards. Rene Matić has spent most of a short career pointing it at the people nearby: family, friends, the community the artist belongs to. Tate, announcing the Turner Prize shortlist in April 2025, described the results as highly personal photographs, shown alongside sound, banners and installation.

From Peterborough to Central Saint Martins

Matić was born in Peterborough in 1997 and graduated in fine art from Central Saint Martins in London in 2020. A series begun two years before that still gives a sense of the approach. Its title is flags for countries that don't exist but bodies that do, and according to Wikipedia it is still going.

In 2022 the South London Gallery showed upon this rock. Two years later CCA Berlin opened AS OPPOSED TO THE TRUTH, which ran from November 2024 to February 2025.

Two prizes for one show

The Berlin show is the one that changed things. It earned Matić a place on the Turner Prize 2025 shortlist, alongside Nnena Kalu, Mohammed Sami and Zadie Xa. University of the Arts London said Matić was the second-youngest artist ever nominated. The four shortlisted artists showed at Cartwright Hall in Bradford, and on 9 December 2025 the prize went to Kalu.

The same exhibition then won the Deutsche Börse Photography Foundation Prize in 2026, worth £30,000, according to 1854 Photography. It is unusual for one show to be recognised by both a general contemporary art prize and a photography prize. That says something about where the work sits: between the photograph on the wall and the room built around it.

What is still private

Little of Matić's work has passed through the art market in public. The one auction record we found is a charity sale: a photograph, Pink Shoes at a Party (2023), offered in a Whitechapel Gallery fundraising sale at Phillips in March 2024 and marked as sold, with no price shown. That is fitting for an artist whose subject is the people closest to them. For now, the pictures are better known than the person behind the camera, and that seems to be the point.

articles.title: Raven Halfmoon's Giants in Clay
articles.summary: A Caddo Nation sculptor from Oklahoma coils stoneware into figures taller than a room. Her first touring show has now visited five venues.
articles.description: The story of Raven Halfmoon, the Caddo Nation ceramic sculptor from Norman, Oklahoma, whose coil-built stoneware figures have toured five American venues and entered museum collections.
articles.body:
Raven Halfmoon builds her sculptures the slow way. She coils clay by hand, ring on ring, then glazes and fires it. The Ogden Museum of Southern Art describes figures ranging from torso size to colossal. One of them, Flagbearer (2022), is made in three stacked sections and stands more than 12 feet tall. The Art Newspaper reports that it took a year to make.

Where she comes from

Halfmoon was born in Norman, Oklahoma, in 1991, and still works there. The Contemporary Austin describes her as a citizen of the Caddo Nation who also has Choctaw, Delaware and Otoe-Missouria heritage. She studied ceramics, painting and cultural anthropology at the University of Arkansas, and later spent two years at the Archie Bray Foundation for the Ceramic Arts in Montana, according to Salon 94.

Many of her figures are women, and many have two faces or more. Walking round them, the face you meet changes.

A show that kept travelling

Her first touring solo exhibition, Flags of Our Mothers, opened at the Aldrich Contemporary Art Museum in Connecticut in June 2023. It moved to the Bemis Center in Omaha in 2024, The Contemporary Austin in 2025 and the Ogden Museum in New Orleans from September 2025 to March 2026. In 2026 it reached Ballroom Marfa in Texas. The same year she showed in the Whitney Biennial.

Museums have bought as well as borrowed. Crystal Bridges acquired Caddo Woman Warrior (2021) in 2024. The Contemporary Austin lists the Detroit Institute of Arts, ICA Miami and the Montclair Art Museum among the collections that hold her work. She was a 2023 Eiteljorg Contemporary Art Fellow and a finalist for the LOEWE Craft Prize in 2024.

Clay and time

Two smaller pieces have sold at Phillips in New York, both in 2024, each for a little over US$20,000 with fees. Those sales say less about her than the year it took to build one figure. Coiling is one of the oldest ways of making a pot. Halfmoon has used it to make some of the largest ceramic figures being shown in American museums today.

articles.title: Dana Awartani and the Slow Work of Repair
articles.summary: Trained in centuries-old crafts, a Palestinian-Saudi artist darns, dyes and stitches to answer destruction. This year she represented Saudi Arabia at Venice.
articles.description: How Dana Awartani, born in Jeddah in 1987, uses traditional Islamic crafts such as darning, natural dyeing and geometry to address loss and repair, from the 2024 Venice Biennale to the Saudi pavilion in 2026.
articles.body:
At the Venice Biennale in 2024, Dana Awartani hung a large expanse of silk that she had dyed with herbs and spices, torn, and then darned by hand. The Biennale's own page connects the work to the destruction of buildings and heritage in Gaza. The tears were made in an instant. The mending took far longer.

A training in old crafts

Awartani was born in Jeddah in 1987 and lives between Jeddah and New York. She is Palestinian-Saudi. After a degree at Central Saint Martins in London, she took an MA at the Prince's Foundation School of Traditional Arts, which teaches crafts such as geometry, illumination and embroidery, according to Ocula.

Those crafts run through everything she makes. Ocula lists painting, sculpture, site-specific installation and performance among her media, often using natural dyes and geometric drawing. In 2021 she received the National Cultural Award from the Saudi Ministry of Culture.

From Venice to Venice

Two years after showing in the main exhibition, she came back to Venice for her country. The Saudi Arabia pavilion at the 61st Biennale, which ran from 9 May to 22 November 2026, was given to Awartani, with Antonia Carver of Art Jameel as curator, according to e-flux. In between, she had a solo exhibition at Arnolfini in Bristol in 2025, built around a work called Standing by the Ruins.

Her work is held by the Guggenheim in New York, the British Museum and the Louvre Abu Dhabi, among others. Lisson Gallery's 2024 page says she is represented by Chemould Prescott Road in Mumbai and Athr Gallery in Jeddah.

Why the slowness matters

It would be quicker to print a pattern than to embroider it, and quicker to bin torn silk than to darn it. Awartani's choice to spend the time is the clearest thing about her work. The repair never hides the damage. It sits on top of it, stitch by stitch.

articles.title: Ana Segovia and the Cowboy, Looked at Again
articles.summary: A Mexico City painter borrows the cowboys and film stars of Mexican popular culture and asks what they say about being a man.
articles.description: The story of Ana Segovia, the Mexico City painter whose work reworks Mexican cowboy imagery and golden-age cinema, from a residency in Oaxaca to MOCA Los Angeles, Venice and Frieze London.
articles.body:
The charro, the Mexican cowboy, is one of the most familiar figures in Mexico's films, songs and posters. Ana Segovia paints him again and again. MOCA Los Angeles describes paintings that take images from Mexican cowboy culture and golden-age cinema and use them to question ideas of masculinity.

Mexico City and Chicago

Segovia was born in Mexico City in 1991 and works there, after studying at the School of the Art Institute of Chicago. In spring 2020 Segovia was resident at Casa Wabi, the artist residency at Puerto Escondido on the Oaxaca coast, according to kurimanzutto.

Most of the work is oil on canvas or linen, some of it very wide. Through Mario's perspective (2024) is 125 cm high and over four metres long. Recent projects add digital video and charcoal drawings.

Three busy years

On 15 November 2023, kurimanzutto announced that Segovia had joined the gallery. What followed was quick. In 2024 Segovia showed at the Venice Biennale and opened a solo exhibition at MOCA Los Angeles, which ran until May 2025. MOCA bought Through Mario's perspective. In 2025 came solo shows at C3A in Córdoba and OK Linz in Austria, and a solo booth with kurimanzutto at Frieze London, which Galerie magazine covered in a profile that November.

This autumn kurimanzutto's New York space showed The Office of Inter-American Affairs Presents, Segovia's first solo exhibition there. The gallery lists works in the Louisiana Museum of Modern Art in Denmark, the Denver Art Museum and the Pérez Art Museum Miami.

The point of borrowing

The poses in these paintings are meant to feel familiar. That is how they work. A viewer who recognises a stance from an old film is already halfway into the question the painting asks: who taught us that this is how a man should stand?

articles.title: Jes Fan and the Body as Material
articles.summary: A glassblower from Hong Kong makes sculptures from resin, glass and substances such as melanin and testosterone. Yale has just surveyed the first ten years.
articles.description: The story of Jes Fan, the sculptor born in Toronto and raised in Hong Kong, whose work in glass, resin and biological materials reached the Venice Biennale, the Whitney Biennial and a 2026 museum survey at Yale.
articles.body:
Read the materials list for Jes Fan's Form Begets Function (2020) and the title starts to make sense. Alongside resin, wood, fibreglass and glass, Andrew Kreps Gallery lists urine, depo-testosterone and melanin. The things that bodies make, and that are often used to sort bodies into groups, become the stuff of sculpture.

Toronto, Hong Kong, Rhode Island

Fan was born in Toronto in 1990 and grew up in Hong Kong. Wallpaper reports that Fan trained in the glass department of the Rhode Island School of Design, and in 2018 took up a residency at Recess in Brooklyn, working with a community biology lab. Fan now works between Brooklyn and Hong Kong.

Glass is still at the centre of the work, alongside resin and 3D prints of body parts. Many pieces look like specimens, or like models from a medical school.

From Venice to Yale

The work was shown in the main exhibition of the 59th Venice Biennale in 2022, in the New Museum Triennial and in the 2024 Whitney Biennial. In 2022 Fan received a grant from the Pollock-Krasner Foundation. The first solo exhibition in New York, Sites of Wounding: Interchapter, opened at Andrew Kreps Gallery in October 2024.

This year Yale University Art Gallery gave Fan a first museum survey, Jes Fan: Unbounded, from 27 February to 28 June 2026, covering roughly the first ten years of work.

Looking closely

Fan's sculptures reward a slow look and a careful read of the label. The forms are often beautiful in the way blown glass can be. What they are made of is less comfortable, and that tension is where the work lives.

articles.title: Two Paintings, Two Long Journeys to the Saleroom
articles.summary: A Van Gogh chestnut tree and a Kandinsky abstract set auction records in New York this November. Their owners over a century tell you why.
articles.description: The stories behind Van Gogh's Châtaigniers en fleurs and Kandinsky's Betonte Ecken, the record-setting lots of November 2026: where they were painted, who owned them, and the 1936 sale that nearly stopped one of them.
articles.body:
Two paintings made the biggest headlines in New York this November. One was painted in a village near Paris in May 1890. The other was painted at a German art school over the winter of 1922. Both had passed through many hands before they reached the saleroom, and the record of those hands tells you a good deal about why people wanted them.

A chestnut tree in Auvers

Vincent van Gogh arrived in Auvers-sur-Oise in May 1890, after a year at the asylum in Saint-Rémy. He wanted, in his words as the Kröller-Müller Museum reports them, to study peasants and landscapes from life. He died there at the end of July. In those few weeks he made around 70 oil paintings.

On 24 May he painted Châtaigniers en fleurs, chestnut trees in full blossom, on a canvas 70 by 58 centimetres. A little earlier he had painted a smaller canvas of the same subject, now in the Kröller-Müller Museum in Otterlo. The museum's own description of that one gives a sense of how he worked: flat strokes of green, short dark blue strokes for the structure of the leaves, a sky of overlapping zigzags.

Where it went next

Sotheby's lot page sets out the owners in order. The painting passed to his brother Theo, then to Theo's widow Johanna and their son. It went through the Berlin dealer Paul Cassirer in 1905, through collectors in Paris, and in 1909 to Samuel Fischer, the Berlin publisher. His widow Hedwig inherited it in 1934. In 1936 it was sold to a couple in Paris. From 1945 it belonged to George and Marie DeSylva in Los Angeles, and in 1975 it was bought by the family of Nelly Arrieta de Blaquier in Argentina.

That 1936 sale came back to matter. The Fischer heirs said the family had sold the painting under Nazi persecution, as the family fled Germany. The day before the auction, Sotheby's said the two families had reached a settlement, and the painting was sold under their agreement. The terms were not made public.

On 18 November it sold for US$190.4 million with fees, as reported by Art Insider and others. It is now the most expensive Van Gogh ever sold at auction.

Corners and circles

Wassily Kandinsky painted Betonte Ecken, or Accented Corners, between December 1922 and January 1923. He had recently started teaching at the Bauhaus. Tate has described his compositions of 1921 to 1935 as tighter and more geometric than what came before, and this one is built from black lines and coloured geometric shapes.

In 1929 it was bought by Hilla Rebay, who gave it to the Guggenheim in 1941. In 1964 the museum sold it in London, one of about 50 Kandinskys sent to auction, for £22,000. It went to a New York dealer, then to collectors in Boston, and in 1986 it sold at Sotheby's New York for US$1 million. Artsy and The Art Newspaper say it was bought then by the family who sold it this year, the Nahmads.

On 17 November it sold at Christie's New York for US$85.8 million with fees, as reported by The Art Newspaper, nearly twice the artist's previous auction record. A month earlier, Christie's in London had sold an earlier Kandinsky, Das bunte Leben of 1907, for £31.56 million.

What the journeys have in common

Both paintings spent decades with one owner. Both have long, written-down histories, the kind that let a buyer see exactly where a picture has been. And both come from moments that mattered in their painters' lives: Van Gogh's last weeks, Kandinsky's first years at the Bauhaus. None of that is a measure of how good a painting is. It does help explain why, on two evenings in New York, more than one person wanted each of them very badly.

articles.title: Who Decides an Artist Matters?
articles.summary: Museums, prizes and the odd auction room moment. A look at how eleven artists we follow came to be taken seriously, and what that recognition leaves out.
articles.description: A reported essay on how artists gain standing through museum shows, prizes and biennials, from Richter and Kusama at Tate Modern to OSGEMEOS, KAWS, Vhils, Eko Nugroho and Faith XLVII.
articles.body:
Ask how an artist becomes important and you get two kinds of answer. One is about the work: what it looks like, how it is made, what it changed. The other is about people: the curators, juries and crowds who decide, over years, which work is worth looking at again. This is a reported essay about the second kind, drawn from museum, prize and press records listed below.

The museum invitation

For many artists the clearest sign of standing is a large museum show. Tate Modern has given several of the artists we write about that moment. Gerhard Richter's retrospective, Panorama, opened there in October 2011, and Tate's announcement described him as widely regarded as one of the most important artists working today. Yayoi Kusama's Infinity Mirror Rooms opened at Tate Modern in May 2021 and stayed until April 2024, close to three years.

El Anatsui was given the Turbine Hall. His Hyundai Commission, Behind the Red Moon, opened in October 2023, and Tate called it the largest work he had made.

Timing can say as much as the invitation. S.H. Raza had worked in France for decades before the Centre Pompidou gave him a retrospective in 2023, seven years after his death. The Art Newspaper described it as his first show in a state-run museum. Beatriz Milhazes had been showing internationally since the 1990s when the Guggenheim opened a show of her work in 2025 and called it the first New York museum exhibition devoted to her. Her work had been seen in New York museums before, in group and project displays: Wikipedia lists MoMA in 2002 and the Jewish Museum in 2016.

Prizes for a whole career

Some honours are given for a single show. Others are given for a life's work. The Praemium Imperiale, awarded in Japan, went to Richter for painting in 1997 and to Kusama in 2006. El Anatsui received the Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement at the Venice Biennale in 2015, and the Praemium Imperiale two years later.

National honours count too, though they are read differently abroad. Raza received India's Padma Shri in 1981, the Padma Bhushan in 2007 and the Padma Vibhushan in 2013. France made him a Commandeur of the Légion d'honneur in 2015.

Artists who started outside

For artists who began on the street, the route in looks different. In 2008 Tate Modern invited six artists, among them the twin brothers known as OSGEMEOS, to make work for its river façade, the first commission to use it. Tate called the show the first major public museum display of street art in London.

Others followed in their own cities and their own time. The Brooklyn Museum gave KAWS a survey of more than 100 works in 2021, from early graffiti drawings to large sculpture. In Lisbon, MAAT showed Vhils' video installation Prisma in 2022, and MUDE, the city's design museum, showed his printed editions in early 2026. Eko Nugroho was one of five artists in Indonesia's pavilion at the Venice Biennale in 2013. In 2025 the STRAAT Museum in Amsterdam showed Faith XLVII with her son and another artist, and added one of her works to its collection.

And then there is Banksy

Banksy is the clearest case of an artist whose standing was built almost entirely outside these systems. His best known moment came in an auction room. In 2018 a shredder hidden in the frame of a Girl with Balloon was set off just after the hammer fell at Sotheby's. Three years later the renamed Love Is in the Bin was sold again at Sotheby's London, and The Art Newspaper reported a price of £18.6m with fees.

What recognition does and does not tell you

A museum show, a prize or a place in a pavilion is a judgement made by particular people at a particular time. It makes the work easier to see and easier to take seriously. It does not settle whether the work is good, and it does not tell you whether you will like it.

It also misses a great deal. Many artists are better known in their own region than in London or New York, and many of the walls these artists painted were never reviewed by anyone. The record above is a starting point for looking, not a ranking.

articles.title: OSGEMEOS, Two Brothers and One World
articles.summary: Twin brothers from São Paulo who started on the walls and never stopped painting the same imagined place.
articles.description: A reported profile of OSGEMEOS: graffiti in São Paulo, a painted Scottish castle and the dream world they carry from walls to canvas.
articles.alt: Two men in caps stand on a New York pavement, one with arms folded and the other looking down at a music player, both in clothes spattered with paint.
articles.credit: Otávio and Gustavo Pandolfo, the twins who work as OSGEMEOS, in New York in April 2007. Photo: Fatima Haidara, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.
articles.body:
OSGEMEOS is a name for two people. Gustavo and Otavio Pandolfo are twin brothers, born in 1974, and the name means “the twins” in Portuguese. This is a reported essay, drawn from the records listed below.

From the street

They started out in graffiti, and Artsy, which tracks their career, names hip-hop and global youth culture among their influences. It also notes that the work draws on Brazilian folk culture as well as the present day. The brothers are represented by Fortes D'Aloia & Gabriel in São Paulo and by Lehmann Maupin.

A castle in Scotland

In May 2007 the London street art blog Hookedblog reported a month-long project at Kelburn Castle in Scotland. OSGEMEOS, Nina Pandolfo and Nunca came from Brazil to paint the castle's walls and turrets alongside Scottish artists, living in the castle while they worked. Four years later Hyperallergic reported that the owners wanted the paint to stay.

The same world, indoors

Their figures are long-limbed and bright yellow. Indoors the brothers add things a wall cannot hold. One 2010 panel at Christie's combined acrylic, spray enamel, latex and sequins. A 2005 work sold by Phillips in May 2025, O dia em que a Andorinha não voou, came with its own audio player and headphones. It made US$101,600.

What is not known

How the two divide the work is not recorded in the sources we read. They sign as one, and we have reported them as one.

articles.title: Vhils and the Portrait in the Wall
articles.summary: A Lisbon artist who makes faces by taking the city apart, one layer at a time.
articles.description: A reported profile of Vhils, Alexandre Farto: Lisbon graffiti, art school in London and a method built on removal.
articles.alt: Vhils, a dark-haired, bearded man in a black T-shirt and dark trousers, standing by a wall of chipped pale plaster with a hammer in his hand, seen from above.
articles.credit: Vhils at work in Beja, Portugal, in 2017. Photo: Nicola Di Nunzio, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.
articles.body:
Most artists add paint. Alexandre Farto, who works as Vhils, takes it away. This is a reported essay. Much of what is known about his career comes from his own website, and we say so where it does.

Lisbon

Farto was born in Lisbon in 1987. His site says he began working in the city as Vhils in the early 2000s, at a time when Lisbon was changing quickly, and that he went on to study in London at Byam Shaw School of Art and Central Saint Martins.

Scratching the surface

His site calls the method subtraction. He cuts, drills, etches or blasts through a surface to bring out an image. The approach was first shown in public at VSP in Lisbon in 2007, and then at the Cans Festival in London in 2008, which the site names as the moment his work became known abroad.

The same idea in the studio

The studio pieces use the street as material. Attrition series #01, sold at Bonhams in London in October 2025 for £10,240, is made of advertising posters collected from the street and carved by hand, 180 by 120 centimetres. The colours of old adverts become the shadows of a face.

What is not known

The site reports work in more than 30 countries. We have not found an independent list to check that against.

articles.title: KAWS and the Cartoon That Grew Up
articles.summary: From bus shelter adverts to a balloon over Manhattan: how Brian Donnelly built a career around one crossed-out face.
articles.description: A reported profile of KAWS, Brian Donnelly: graffiti, animation work, the COMPANION toy and the move from street to sculpture.
articles.body:
KAWS is the name Brian Donnelly, born in 1974, chose to write on walls. According to Christie's, he chose it because he liked how the four letters looked together. This is a reported essay, drawn from the records listed below.

Walls, then adverts

Donnelly studied illustration at the School of Visual Arts in New York and then worked as a background painter on television cartoons, including Doug, Daria and 101 Dalmatians. He tagged buildings in New Jersey and Manhattan, then turned to advertising. Christie's describes him taking posters down from bus shelters and walls, painting his own figures into them at home, and putting them back the next day.

A toy with crossed-out eyes

In 1999, on a visit to Japan with the brand Bounty Hunter, he made his first toy, COMPANION. Christie's reports that the edition of 500 sold out almost at once. The figure, with X's for eyes, became the centre of his work.

Bigger and bigger

In 2012 a COMPANION balloon floated through Manhattan in the Macy's Thanksgiving parade. In 2019 a 37 metre inflatable lay in Hong Kong's Victoria Harbour. A fibreglass COMPANION of 2011, offered at Christie's in June 2026, stands almost two and a half metres tall.

Where he sits

Christie's notes that many people, the curator Michael Auping among them, compare him with Basquiat and Haring, who also came from the street, and with Warhol and Koons. He names Takashi Murakami's collaborations as an influence. Whether a cartoon on this scale is still a joke is a question his work keeps open.

articles.title: Eko Nugroho, Masks and Thread
articles.summary: A Yogyakarta artist whose masked comic figures turn up on walls, in embroidery and in a national museum.
articles.description: A reported profile of Eko Nugroho: Yogyakarta, community projects, masked figures and the move from paint to thread.
articles.body:
Eko Nugroho was born in Yogyakarta, Indonesia, in 1977, and still lives and works there. This is a reported essay, drawn from the museum and auction house records listed below.

Working with others

The Singapore Art Museum describes him as an artist who often works with communities and other creatives to draw attention to social issues. He works in painting, embroidery and sculpture, and Phillips has sold his work in batik on cotton.

Why the masks

His figures come from comics, and many of them wear masks. The museum gives a reason: he avoids stereotyped faces that could lead to discriminatory readings of his work.

From wall to thread

In Illusion (2007), now in the Singapore Art Museum, a masked figure stands in a stripped landscape full of monster-like machines. The museum reads it as a picture of environmental “crispy crisis”. It is made in embroidery, nearly three metres tall, and it keeps the flat, bold look of a drawing on a wall.

On the map

He showed at the 5th Asia Pacific Triennial in Brisbane in 2006, and later in the Singapore Art Museum's Imaginarium in 2017 and the Children's Biennale at National Gallery Singapore in 2019.

articles.title: Faith XLVII, From Faith47 to 39 Countries
articles.summary: A South African graffiti writer who took her quiet figures from local walls to murals around the world.
articles.description: A reported profile of Faith XLVII: graffiti in South Africa from 1997, murals in 39 countries and a practice that grew beyond the wall.
articles.alt: A tall painted figure in a dark hooded robe, face lifted and lit from one side, fills the pale green end wall of a block of flats. Bare trees stand in front and ivy climbs the brick beside it.
articles.credit: Mural by Faith XLVII on the end wall of a block of flats in Cologne, photographed in February 2015. Photo: Raimond Spekking, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.
articles.body:
Faith XLVII was born in 1979 and began writing graffiti on South African streets in 1997, under the name Faith47. This is a reported essay, drawn from the auction house records listed below.

Leaving home

In 2006, according to Strauss & Co, she began travelling to paint public murals. The count now stands at 39 countries. One of them is Capax Infiniti, painted in 2014 on the side of the Carlyle building in Portland, Oregon.

Beyond the wall

Her work has grown into new media installations, hand-sewn wall tapestries, bronzes about hierarchies of power, paintings and prints. Wall images come back as prints: the Portland mural later became a lithograph with the same name.

Three words

One triptych, sold by Strauss & Co in June 2024, is called Coltan; Oil; Diamonds. Three resources mined in Africa, each on a panel 230 centimetres tall in a wooden frame she made by hand. It joins the quiet, almost religious mood of her figures to a hard subject.

Where it is seen

Strauss lists her work in collections including Universal Studios in Los Angeles and the Cyril Ramaphosa Foundation, and shows at the Brooklyn Museum, the Calais Museum of Fine Art and the Bernard Magrez Foundation in France.

articles.title: Yayoi Kusama, One Mark Over and Over
articles.summary: The Japanese artist who died in August 2026 spent more than six decades repeating the same marks until they filled canvases, objects and rooms.
articles.description: A reported profile of Yayoi Kusama: Kyoto training, the New York Infinity Nets, the dots and mirror rooms, and the record set at Sotheby's in November 2026.
articles.alt: Close view of Yayoi Kusama's face, with dark hair, red lipstick and pale pink glasses in a decorative silver frame.
articles.credit: Yayoi Kusama, around 2004. A still from George Quasha's film series art is (Speaking Portraits). Photo: George Quasha, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.
articles.body:
Yayoi Kusama died in a Tokyo hospital on 14 August 2026, aged 97. Her foundation announced the death on 27 August. Three months later one of her earliest paintings set a new auction record for her work. The gap between those two facts says something about how long the paintings took to be understood.

Matsumoto

She was born in Matsumoto in 1929. Her family were merchants who ran a plant nursery and seed farm, and as a schoolgirl she drew pumpkins. From about the age of ten she had hallucinations. Her mother disapproved of the drawing and took her materials away.

At thirteen she was sent to work in a military factory making parachutes. Her Tokyo dealer told The Art Newspaper that those wartime teenage years shaped her.

Kyoto, then America

In 1948 she studied Japanese-style painting in Kyoto. Before she left Japan she destroyed many of her early works. She went first to Seattle, where she showed at the Zoe Dusanne Gallery in 1957, and after about a year moved on to New York. She stayed there until 1973. She corresponded with Georgia O'Keeffe, and by 1961 her studio was in the same building as Donald Judd and Eva Hesse, who became a close friend.

The Net

The New York paintings are the Infinity Nets: canvases covered edge to edge in looped brushmarks. There is no centre and no border to the pattern. It stops only where the canvas stops. One of them, No. 3P.B. of 1960, was shown in the Whitney Museum's annual exhibition in 1961. On 16 November 2026 it sold at Sotheby's New York for about US$15 million with fees, according to The Art Newspaper.

From net to dot to room

The same repeated mark later became the dot, carried onto pumpkins, sculptures and whole rooms. In the mirror rooms the repetition has no end at all. She first showed at the Venice Biennale in 1966, with Narcissus Garden, a field of mirrored spheres that she sold to visitors for about two dollars each until she was stopped. In 1993 she represented Japan there.

Tokyo

She returned to Japan in 1973. From 1977 she lived, by her own choice, in a mental health hospital in Tokyo, and stayed a resident there for the rest of her life. She went on working. My Eternal Soul, a series of about 900 paintings, occupied her from 2009 to 2021.

What is not settled

Reports of the November sale disagree on which earlier record it replaced. Artsy names a 2022 sale at Phillips; HENI News names a 2023 sale in Hong Kong. We have not tried to settle it.

articles.title: Beatriz Milhazes, Painting Without a Brush
articles.summary: The Rio painter paints on plastic and presses the paint onto canvas, building pictures out of flowers, circles and Carnival colour.
articles.description: A reported profile of Beatriz Milhazes: the 1980s Generation, the plastic-sheet method, and the Brazilian sources behind her patterns.
articles.body:
Beatriz Milhazes paints her pictures twice. First she paints her motifs on plastic sheets. Once the paint is dry, she glues each sheet face down onto the canvas and peels the plastic away, so that only the paint stays behind. The surface that results is smooth, with no brushstrokes, and carries small irregularities from the transfer.

Rio de Janeiro

She was born in Rio de Janeiro in 1960 and still works there, in a studio that overlooks the city's Botanical Garden. She is associated with the 1980s Generation of Brazilian painters, and from 1986 to 1996 she taught painting at the Parque Lage school. The transfer method grew out of research into printing that she began in the 1980s.

A slow method

The sheets are kept and reused, some for as long as ten years, so a motif from an old picture can turn up in a new one. She has compared her steady working routine to that of a bank worker.

Where it has been seen

She showed at the Carnegie International in 1995 and in Brazil's pavilion at the Venice Biennale in 2003. A survey of her work opened at the Pérez Art Museum Miami in September 2014 and ran into 2015.

What goes into the pattern

Wikipedia lists Bridget Riley, Tarsila do Amaral, Georgia O'Keeffe and Elizabeth Murray among her influences. Phillips' lot essay for Paraty (2001 to 2002) adds Baroque architecture, lace, Carnival decoration and the plants of Rio's Botanical Garden. Wikipedia also links her to Antropofagia, the Brazilian modernist idea of taking in outside influences and making them local.

How to look

Find the geometry first, the bands and circles, then watch the flowers slide over and under them. The pictures are crowded on purpose.

articles.title: S.H. Raza, From the Village to the Dot
articles.summary: An Indian painter who spent most of his working life in France moved from landscapes of Provence and Corsica to the bindu, a single point.
articles.description: A reported profile of S.H. Raza: the Progressive Artists' Group, Paris, the French landscapes and the Bindu paintings from 1980.
articles.alt: S.H. Raza, an elderly man with white hair and glasses in a pale suit, seated and leaning over a sheet of paper as people gather close around him.
articles.credit: S.H. Raza at an art summit in Delhi, January 2011. Photo: Chetan Nikam, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.
articles.body:
S.H. Raza's paintings begin with villages and end with a dot. The distance between the two took him most of a working life, much of it spent far from India.

Kakkaiya

Sayed Haider Raza was born in 1922 in Kakkaiya, in what is now Madhya Pradesh. His father, Sayed Mohammed Razi, was a deputy forest ranger, and his mother was Tahira Begum. He was drawing by the age of twelve. Wikipedia records a story from his schooldays: to help him concentrate, a teacher drew a dot on the blackboard. Decades later the dot came back.

Bombay

He trained in Nagpur and at the Sir J. J. School of Art in Bombay. In 1946 he had his first solo show, at the Bombay Art Society Salon, and won its silver medal. In 1947, the year his mother died, he was among the founders of the Progressive Artists' Group, with K. H. Ara and F. N. Souza.

France

Saffronart's catalogue records that in 1948 he met the photographer Henri Cartier-Bresson, who advised him to study Cézanne. In 1950 he went to Paris on a French government scholarship and studied at the École des Beaux-Arts. In 1956 he became the first artist from outside France to win the Prix de la Critique. In 1959 he married Janine Mongillat, who died in 2002.

He travelled to Chartres, Avignon and Aix, and the French landscapes of those years are built of thick impasto. Village Otta Corse (1958), a village in Corsica, is one. In the 1960s he moved away from that Cubist structure, as in La Provence Noire (1965).

The bindu

From 1980 the bindu, a single point, sits at the centre of his work, with circles, triangles and bands of colour around it. He came to speak of it as the centre of his life. He moved back to India late in life (Wikipedia gives both 2010 and 2011) and died in New Delhi in July 2016.

articles.title: Gerhard Richter, the Blur and the Squeegee
articles.summary: The German painter has worked in two strands at once: photographs copied and blurred, and abstracts left partly to chance.
articles.description: A reported profile of Gerhard Richter: Dresden, the move west in 1961, Capitalist Realism, the photo paintings and the squeegee abstracts.
articles.alt: Portrait of Gerhard Richter, an older man with white hair, a short white beard and round dark glasses, in a dark coat, looking at the camera.
articles.credit: Gerhard Richter at the National Gallery, Prague, in April 2017. Photo: Jindřich Nosek (NoJin), CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.
articles.body:
Gerhard Richter has never settled on one way to paint. For most of his career he has worked in two strands side by side, and each seems to argue with the other.

Dresden

He was born in Dresden in 1932 and grew up in Reichenau and Waltersdorf, where his father, Horst, was a village teacher. He left school after the tenth grade and trained as an advertising and stage-set painter. His first application to the Dresden Academy of Fine Arts, in 1950, was turned down as "too bourgeois". He was accepted in 1951.

East to West

In 1961, two months before the Berlin Wall went up, he left for West Germany. In Düsseldorf he studied under Karl Otto Götz, alongside Sigmar Polke and Konrad Lueg, and with them took up the label Capitalist Realism. He has lived in Cologne since 1983.

The blur

The first strand starts with a photograph, copied onto canvas and blurred. Kerze (Candle) of 1982 is one, painted from a photograph he took himself, and part of a group of candles and skulls he painted in 1982 and 1983. The Art Newspaper reports that it sold at Christie's New York in May 2026, from the collection of the dealer Marian Goodman, for US$35 million with fees.

The squeegee

The second strand is abstract. He first titled a work Abstract Painting in 1976, and from the mid-1980s he dragged layers of paint across the canvas with a large homemade squeegee, so that colours scrape, tear and show through. Abstraktes Bild of 1991, two metres tall, is an example. TheValue reports that it sold at Christie's Hong Kong in March 2026 for HK$92.1 million with fees.

Since 1989 he has also dragged wet paint across photographs, putting the two strands into one object. The artist sets the conditions; the paint decides the details.

articles.title: Banksy, the Artist Who Isn't There
articles.summary: No confirmed name, no public face. How an anonymous artist from Bristol built a body of work, and a way of proving it is his.
articles.description: A reported profile of Banksy: the Bristol beginnings, the early move to canvas, Pest Control and the joke as a method, drawn from museum and auction house records.
articles.alt: A dark statue seen from below against a grey sky: a man in a suit strides off the edge of a stone plinth while a large flag he holds blows back over his face, with scaffolded buildings behind.
articles.credit: Statue by Banksy in Waterloo Place, London, installed in April 2026. Photographed in May 2026. Photo: Bex Walton, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.
articles.body:
Banksy works anonymously. For an artist whose canvases now sell for millions, that is an unusual position, and it shapes how everything else about him is known. This is a reported essay: it draws on museum and auction house records, listed below, not on any meeting with the artist.

Bristol first

The record begins in Bristol. A research guide from the Jordan Schnitzer Museum of Art says he started painting graffiti there as a teenager in the 1990s and later moved to London. Phillips, in its catalogue, says his work began to appear on trains and walls in 1993.

The stencil came early. It is quick to use and the image it leaves reads at once, which suits work made in public, at speed, by someone who would rather not be seen making it.

From the wall to the canvas

The move indoors happened sooner than many assume. Laugh Now, a canvas of a chimpanzee wearing a sandwich board that says one day they will be in charge, was painted in 2001 and bought from the artist that same year, according to Bonhams. A year later the same image ran six metres long on a wall commissioned by the Ocean Rooms nightclub in Brighton. The canvas sold at Bonhams in October 2026 for £320,500.

In September 2006 he held a three-day show in Los Angeles called Barely Legal, which included a live elephant, painted. Angel, a canvas in spray paint and emulsion 213 centimetres square, was shown there and was bought by its owner directly from the artist. It sold at Bonhams on 18 November 2026 for US$1,398,200.

A name that certifies

An anonymous artist still needs a way to say what is his. Banksy's answer is Pest Control, his own authentication body. Every recent auction lot we checked, from Laugh Now to a small cut-out canvas of a rat reaching for a red heart, came with its certificate.

That arrangement turns the absent artist into a kind of signature. The work is known to be his because his office says so, not because anyone has watched him make it.

The joke as a method

Rats, chimpanzees and children recur because they let him point at people without drawing them. Bonhams' catalogue calls the chimpanzee a stand-in through which human hierarchies can be seen. The humour comes first, and the point a second later.

The best-known joke was played on the art market itself. In October 2018 a framed Girl with Balloon was partly shredded by a device in its frame moments after it sold at Sotheby's London. The work was renamed Love Is in the Bin.

What is not known

Quite a lot. Auction houses do not even agree on his year of birth: Bonhams catalogues him as born in 1974 on one lot and 1975 on another. We have not tried to settle that, or the question of who he is. The work, at least, is on the record.

articles.title: When an Artist Is Also a Celebrity
articles.summary: A famous name gets the work seen. It also means most people have made up their minds before they look.
articles.description: Fame opens gallery doors and closes minds. An essay on celebrity artists, from Warhol to Amanza Smith, and how to look at their work fairly.
articles.body:
There are two kinds of famous artist. One becomes well known because of the art. The other is well known already and then begins to show art. The art world tends to admire the first and distrust the second.

Fame made by art

Andy Warhol is the model for the first kind. He treated fame as a material. He painted film stars, ran a studio that was also a social scene, founded a magazine and turned himself into one of the most recognisable figures of his century.

Britain had its own version in the 1990s. Damien Hirst put a shark in a tank. Tracey Emin showed her own unmade bed. Both became household names, known to people who had never been inside a gallery.

In these cases the celebrity grew out of the work, and nobody now doubts that they were artists first.

Fame that arrives first

The second kind has a harder time. Amanza Smith was known to television audiences from the series Selling Sunset before she showed a painting. When she made her debut at MASH Gallery in Los Angeles, the gallery described her as multifaceted, and listed roles from model and actress to interior designer and mental health advocate.

Her canvases are layered and full of colour, with pages of her own writing, graffiti-like marks and, in recent work, robotic forms. In April 2025 they were shown in Palma at the opening of a Grove Gallery space, beside work by Zara Muse and Silent Mike.

The suspicion such artists meet is easy to understand. Galleries want visitors, and a famous name brings them. So people wonder whether the work would be on the wall without it.

The opposite choice

It is striking how many artists run the other way. Konn Artiss is anonymous. Zen Xander's own website says that “no single artist's personality sits above the work”. These artists have looked at fame and decided it would get in the way.

So the same art world holds people who are known and want to be judged as artists, and artists who refuse to be known at all.

Looking fairly

How should a viewer handle this? Not by pretending the name is absent. You cannot unknow who made a picture.

But you can notice what the name is doing to your judgement. If you would walk past the work with an unknown signature, fame is flattering it. If you would stop for it and are dismissing it because of who made it, fame is costing it. Both are errors.

The fair test is the dull one. Give it the time you would give anything else. Look at the colour, the surface, the decisions. Then ask whether you would want to see it again.

A longer view

Time settles most of these questions. Celebrity fades faster than paint. In fifty years few people will remember who was on which television programme, and the pictures will have to manage alone. That is the real test, and it applies to everyone.

articles.title: Why Collectors Buy Faces
articles.summary: A landscape gives you somewhere to look. A portrait looks back. That may be the whole explanation.
articles.description: Portraits are among the most sought-after works in contemporary art. An essay on why people want to live with a painted face.
articles.body:
Ask people what art they would hang at home and many will say a view: sea, hills, a street they love. Yet some of the most talked-about sales in contemporary art are of faces. It is worth asking why.

The oldest subject

For most of history a portrait was bought by the person in it. It recorded rank, marked a marriage or kept a likeness after death. The buyer and the subject were the same household.

Today that link has almost gone. Collectors buy portraits of strangers, of public figures, of people the artist knows and they never will.

What the market shows

The prices suggest the appetite is real. Art Plugged reported that Zara Muse's portrait of Malala Yousafzai sold at Bonhams in London in April 2025 for £51,200 including premium. Ocula records that Amoako Boafo's The Lemon Bathing Suit made £675,000 at auction in 2020, a year after it was painted.

Museums tell the same story. In 2018 the National Portrait Gallery in London showed Njideka Akunyili Crosby's series The Beautyful Ones. In 2024 the Belvedere in Vienna gave Boafo more than fifty works' worth of wall.

A caution is due. A handful of results is not a study of the market, and we do not claim that portraits outsell everything else. These are examples of demand, nothing more.

Three reasons

Why would someone want a stranger's face in the sitting room? We can suggest three reasons.

The first is company. A room with a portrait in it has someone else in it. People who live with one often talk about it as a presence.

The second is values. To hang a portrait of Malala Yousafzai is to say something about what you admire. Muse has said she chose the subject for bravery and strength. The buyer is choosing those too.

The third is recognition. For a long time the faces on gallery walls were drawn from a narrow slice of the world. Boafo began his portraits of Black sitters after moving to Vienna, where, Colección SOLO notes, he met racism and stereotyping. “I want to be seen, not the stereotype,” he has said. For many collectors, buying such a portrait is a way of widening who gets seen.

The hand in the face

There is a fourth reason, which has to do with how these pictures are made. Muse builds faces with a knife. Boafo paints skin with his fingers. Akunyili Crosby fills hers with transferred photographs.

In each case the making is visible in the face itself. In a time when any image can be produced in seconds, a face that clearly took a person days to make has a pull of its own.

Looking back

The simplest answer may still be the best. We are built to look at faces. We read them before we can read anything else. A painted face, hung where you pass it every day, never quite becomes furniture.

articles.title: The Artist's Name as a Brand
articles.summary: Zara Muse, Zen Xander, Konn Artiss, Vhils, JR, Mr Dot. Count how many of the artists in these pages work under a name they chose.
articles.description: Working names, pseudonyms and collectives: how contemporary artists use a name as a shield, a signature and a brand.
articles.body:
Artists have always signed their work. What is newer is how many now sign it with a name that is not on their passport.

A name as a shield

Some choose a working name for privacy. Zara Muse is the professional name of Alexandra Johnson, who has said it gives her a degree of separation between her life and her work. The paintings can travel to hotels, auctions and other countries. The person can stay at home.

Others go further and withhold the person altogether. Konn Artiss is anonymous. JR works under his initials alone. In both cases the secrecy has a practical side, since much of the work is done in public without asking.

A name as a tag

For artists who began in graffiti, the chosen name comes first. Vhils is the name Alexandre Farto has used since he began painting graffiti at thirteen in Seixal, on the edge of Lisbon. A tag is a signature designed to be written fast and recognised at a distance. That is also a fair description of a logo.

A name as a group

A name does not have to belong to one person. Zen Xander has been described in the press as an anonymous street artist. The artist's own website says it is a small collective of painters, illustrators, designers and writers who share a belief that art should be warm, humorous and relatable.

That is less strange than it sounds. The workshops of the old masters turned out paintings under one name with many hands involved. El Anatsui's vast hangings are assembled by teams. The single signature has often stood for a studio.

A name as a character

Then there are names that work as characters. Clarke Reynolds, who makes art from braille, also appears as Mr Dot, a figure he uses to reach children. The name does a job the artist's own could not.

When the name becomes the product

Once a name is recognised, it can be attached to things. Limited edition prints, signed and numbered, are the simplest case. Hotel residencies are another. Fashion is a third: in 2020 Amoako Boafo worked with Dior on its spring and summer 2021 menswear collection, which printed his paintings across the clothes.

None of this is new. Andy Warhol understood sixty years ago that an artist's name could work like a company's. What has changed is the speed. A name can now go from a wall to a product in a couple of years.

What to make of it

It is tempting to be cynical. A chosen name can look like marketing, and sometimes it is.

But there is another way to see it. A working name lets the art be judged a little more on its own. It protects people who would not otherwise show their work. It lets several people speak with one voice. The name on the label is a decision, like every other decision in the picture, and it is worth asking what it is doing there.

articles.title: From Gallery Wall to Hotel Wall: The Gallery in Residence
articles.summary: A hotel used to buy its art once and hang it for twenty years. Now some are borrowing a gallery instead.
articles.description: Galleries are placing changing displays of art in hotels. A feature on the gallery in residence model, with Silent Mike at Dorsett Shepherds Bush as a case study.
articles.body:
Walk into most hotels and the art is part of the fit-out, chosen with the carpet and expected to last as long. A different arrangement has been spreading. A gallery takes over the walls, hangs a show, and a few months later hangs another.

How it works

The idea is borrowed from the artist residency, where a maker is given a place to work for a set time. Here it is the gallery, or one of its artists, that takes up residence. The hotel gets a changing display it did not have to buy. The gallery gets a second set of walls and a new audience walking past them.

A west London example

In March 2025 the Dorsett hotel in Shepherds Bush announced a partnership with Grove Gallery and named its first artist in residence: Silent Mike.

Art Plugged reported that the show, Chromatic Shift, placed fifteen works through the hotel's main bar and restaurant and opened to the public on 28 March. It was a change of direction for the artist. His 2023 debut at Quantus Gallery in London, Introspective, had been entirely in black and white. The new pieces were in full colour.

The method is worth describing. According to the same report, each piece is built from machine-cut wooden circles with hand-sanded surfaces, finished in layers of paint, primer and a glossy paste. The hotel described intricate geometric patterns combined with elements of classical sculpture, and Art Plugged named Michelangelo and Bernini as reference points.

The hotel's announcement made two promises that matter. The artist would be present to talk about his process, and more artists would follow.

Not a one-off

The same gallery lists a rolling residency at South Place Hotel in east London, with work by Zen Xander, Frank Canvas and Robi Walters. It records a three-month Zara Muse exhibition at a venue called Shanghai Noir in 2024. FAD Magazine reported a year-long display of fourteen of her works at Fairmont Windsor Park.

Residency or decoration

What separates a residency from simply renting out pictures? Three things, we would suggest.

The first is change. If the work never rotates, it is décor. The second is the artist. A residency should mean the maker is named, credited and now and then in the room. The third is information. A guest should be able to find out what they are looking at without asking at reception.

What it means for artists

For an artist early in a career, a hotel offers something a small gallery cannot: hundreds of people a day with time on their hands. For the visitor it removes the awkwardness some feel about walking into a gallery at all.

The cost is control. A bar is noisy, the lighting is for atmosphere and nobody came for the art. Work shown there has to hold its own without help.

That is not a bad test. A picture that can stop someone on the way to breakfast is doing something right.

articles.title: Who Owns the Street? Public Art With and Without Permission
articles.summary: Some public art is commissioned. Some appears overnight. The interesting question is who gets to say yes.
articles.description: Public art is made with permission, without it, or somewhere in between. A feature on JR, Vhils, Konn Artiss and the question of who gets to decide.
articles.body:
A painting in a gallery has a simple chain of permission. The gallery owns the wall and chose the work. Step outside and it gets complicated at once. The wall has an owner. The street has a council. The neighbours have opinions. And the artist may not have asked any of them.

Three kinds of yes

It helps to separate three permissions that are often lumped together. There is the law, which decides whether marking a surface is a crime. There is the owner, who may or may not want a picture on their building. And there are the people who live with it every day.

These do not always agree. A legal mural can be resented by a whole street. An illegal one can be loved.

The case for not asking

The French artist JR has been frank about which permission matters to him. He told Elephant magazine that if the people in a place agree to a project, an official in an office should not be able to stop it, and that this is why much of his work is done illegally.

His project in Rio de Janeiro in 2008 shows the idea at its limit. To paste portraits of local women across a hillside favela, he went to the people who actually controlled the area, explained what he wanted to do and was eventually allowed in.

The same artist, invited

Eight years later JR was back in Rio with full official blessing. For the 2016 Olympics he made The Giants, enormous images of athletes fitted to particular buildings. Same city, same artist, opposite arrangement.

That is the usual path. Vhils began as a teenage graffiti writer and now carves walls at festivals and on commission. Zen Xander is described as moving from the street to the gallery. Yesterday's trespass becomes today's invitation.

The uninvited guest

Then there is the artist who turns up at someone else's event. In October 2025, Konn Artiss left five blocks of ice outside the entrance to Frieze London, each holding a small figure of a famous artist. The published reports do not say whether anyone gave permission. The title, ANTI-FRIEZE, suggests what the answer would have been.

The work only makes sense in that spot. Move it to a gallery and it is a sculpture. Outside the fair, uninvited, it is a comment.

What permission changes

Permission is not neutral. A commissioned mural has been approved, which means someone decided it was safe. That is no insult to the work, but it shapes what can be said.

Work made without asking carries a risk that the commissioned kind does not, and viewers can feel it. The risk is also real for other people: the owner who has to clean a wall, the resident who never wanted a giant face outside the window.

A better question

So who owns the street? In law, the answer is clear enough. In practice, the street belongs to whoever uses it, and public art is one long argument about that.

The fairest test may be the one JR points to. Do the people who live with the work want it there? If they do, the paperwork tends to follow. If they do not, no amount of official approval will make it theirs.

articles.title: Vhils and the Art of Taking Away
articles.summary: Nearly every picture ever made was made by adding something to a surface. Vhils makes his by taking the surface away.
articles.description: Vhils carves portraits into city walls with chisels and jackhammers. A feature on the Portuguese artist and an art made by removing, not adding.
articles.alt: A large portrait of a man in a cap, made by chipping away the pale plaster of a tall brown city wall to show the darker layers beneath.
articles.credit: Joe Hatchiban, a wall portrait carved by Vhils (Alexandre Farto) in Berlin in 2011. Photographed in 2013. Photo: OTFW, Berlin, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.
articles.body:
On the side of a worn building, a face several metres high looks out from the plaster. There is no paint on it. The light parts are where the old render still clings. The dark parts are where it has been cut back to brick.

This is the work of Alexandre Farto, who signs himself Vhils. He was born in 1987 and grew up in Seixal, an industrial suburb of Lisbon.

A boy with a spray can

He started writing graffiti at thirteen. His gallery tells how the walls around him were already crowded. After the revolution of 1974, Portuguese walls filled with political murals, and in the decades that followed those were buried under advertising, posters and more paint. A wall in his neighbourhood was a stack of years.

He later studied in London, at Byam Shaw and Central Saint Martins. The idea he arrived at was simple and odd. If the wall is made of layers, the picture is already in there. You only have to dig.

Scratching the Surface

He gave the method a plain name. By his own account, Scratching the Surface was first shown in Lisbon in 2007 and reached an international audience at the Cans Festival in London in 2008.

The process starts like a stencil. He marks out the portrait on the wall, deciding what will stay and what will go. Then the tools come out: chisels, hammers, drills, jackhammers. Reports of his work list acid and small explosive charges as well. What is left is a face in low relief, made of the wall's own history.

Whose faces

The people in the portraits are rarely famous. His gallery describes them as anonymous city dwellers, and notes that the walls he chooses are neglected or abandoned ones. A person nobody would paint, on a wall nobody would look at. The pairing is the point.

He has a phrase for what he does: an archaeology of the present.

Beyond the wall

The same thinking runs through his other work. In the studio he peels back layers of posters salvaged from the street. He has etched metal, carved wood and made pieces with controlled explosions. In each case the image comes from removing material.

The carved walls now appear in cities from Moscow to Sydney, and he has shown in galleries in London, Paris and Hong Kong.

Why it stays with you

Most public art puts something new in front of you. A Vhils portrait shows you what was already there, under the paint and the posters. It treats the city as a record that can be read.

It is also honest about time. The wall will keep crumbling. One day the face will go the way of everything else that was ever on that surface. Until then it looks back at the street that made it.

articles.title: Clarke Reynolds: Braille You Can See
articles.summary: Braille is written to be felt. Clarke Reynolds also wants it seen, in colour, at the size of a wall.
articles.description: Clarke Reynolds turns braille into colourful visual art meant to be touched. A note on how the work is made and who it is for.
articles.body:
Most art comes with a rule: do not touch. Clarke Reynolds makes work that asks for the opposite.

Losing sight

Reynolds was born in Havant and is based in Portsmouth. He has said he knew at six that he wanted to be a professional artist, and Envision reports that Franz Marc's painting The Yellow Cow was an early inspiration. He lost the sight in his right eye as a child. In his early thirties he was diagnosed with retinitis pigmentosa, a degenerative eye condition.

He studied model making at degree level, and Euronews reported that he worked as a dental model maker until his sight made the job impossible. He kept making art and changed how he did it.

Dots as a language

Braille builds each letter from a cell of up to six raised dots. Reynolds takes that system and enlarges it. The dots become painted circles in strong colours, set out in the patterns of real letters and words. Sighted visitors see a field of colour. Anyone who reads braille can read what it says.

The colours are chosen, not random. Euronews reported that he links them to how common each letter is, alongside ordinary colour theory, and that sighted visitors to his London show were given glasses that imitate sight loss.

In the text of one piece, quoted by Arts Help, he introduces himself as a blind visual artist for whom braille is his "artistic language".

So the work operates twice. It is a picture and it is a sentence, and different people get to it by different routes.

Meant to be decoded

In 2021 he showed Decoding Braille, Decoding Me at the Yellow Edge Gallery in Gosport, a show RNIB Connect Radio called his first solo exhibition. He described two visitors, one visually impaired and one sighted, spending about three hours racing each other to decode the works.

Accounts differ on which show came first. Euronews and Arts Help both describe his exhibition at the Quantus Gallery in London, in early 2023, as his first solo show. In February 2024 Grove Gallery showed 5° of Vision, which mixed braille with 1980s video games such as Pac-Man, Tetris and Space Invaders. Later that year the Envision Arts Gallery in Wichita gave him his first solo show in the United States, with braille workshops in local schools alongside it.

Bigger dots

The scale keeps growing. In Tallahassee, Florida, in 2022, a local station reported dots three feet across, each the size of a pavement square, spelling the word love.

Who it is for

Reynolds also works under the name Mr Dot, a character he uses with children, and Paths to Literacy has written about the Mr Dot book for young readers. The Big Issue reported that he works around 70 hours a week and is campaigning for braille to be taught in schools, as the system passes its two hundredth year.

The argument in the work is plain. A gallery that only lets you look has already decided who its visitors are. Change the material, and the audience changes with it.

articles.title: Paper, Paste and Scale: The Craft Behind JR's Street Portraits
articles.summary: A camera, a big printer, a bucket of paste and a wall. JR's method is simple enough that he has given it away.
articles.description: How JR makes his giant street portraits: black-and-white photographs, large-format paper and paste. A note on the craft and on the Inside Out Project.
articles.body:
The French artist JR, born in Paris in 1983, describes himself with a word of his own: photograffeur, part photographer and part graffiti writer. He takes portraits, prints them very large in black and white and pastes them onto buildings.

Three ingredients

The method has barely changed. First a photograph, usually a face, shot close. Then the print, on plain paper in strips large enough to cover a wall. Then the paste, brushed on by hand, often by teams of volunteers.

Each part is cheap. None of it is permanent. Rain and sun take the paper off within months. That is not a flaw in the work. A pasted portrait is closer to an event than to a monument.

Why so big

Scale does the arguing. A passport-sized face asks nothing of you. The same face six storeys high is hard to pass without wondering who it is.

His early series Portraits of a Generation, made between 2004 and 2006, showed young people from the housing estates around Paris in huge format. For Face 2 Face, the Brooklyn Museum records, he and his collaborators pasted large portraits side by side on both the Israeli and Palestinian sides of the separation wall.

Giving the method away

In 2011 JR won the TED Prize, worth 100,000 dollars, and used it to start the Inside Out Project. The idea was to hand his process to anyone who wanted it.

It works like this. A group takes its own portraits and sends them in. JR's studio prints them as posters and ships them back. The group pastes them up wherever it chooses. The Brooklyn Museum's exhibition text adds that with photobooth trucks, people can have a portrait taken and receive the poster straight away.

The numbers are large. According to Wikipedia, by August 2022 there had been more than 2,300 group actions, with nearly half a million posters sent to 148 countries.

What the craft teaches

There is a lesson here for anyone who thinks ambitious art needs expensive materials. JR's kit could be bought on any high street. What makes the work is the decision about whose face goes where, and the labour of many people with brushes and ladders.

Paper, paste and scale. The rest is permission, or the lack of it.

articles.title: El Anatsui and the Second Life of Materials
articles.summary: Flatten a bottle cap, punch a hole in it, wire it to the next one. Repeat a few hundred thousand times.
articles.description: El Anatsui turns thousands of discarded bottle caps into vast hanging sculptures. A note on how they are made and why the material matters.
articles.alt: A weathered grey stone sculpture of a crouching, rounded figure whose large hands cover its face, set on paving in front of a yellow concrete building.
articles.credit: Ambivalent Hold, from a design by El Anatsui, made by the SKEP art collective for the Physical Sciences building at the University of Nigeria, Nsukka. Photographed in 2024. Photo: Mercyjamb123, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.
articles.body:
From a distance, an El Anatsui hanging looks like cloth of gold. It folds and ripples and catches the light. Walk up to it and you find it is made of rubbish: the aluminium caps and collars from liquor bottles, each one flattened and wired to its neighbours.

Anyako

Anatsui was born in Anyako, in the Volta Region of Ghana, in 1944. Wikipedia records that he was the youngest of his father's 32 children, that he lost his mother and was brought up by an uncle, and that his first brush with art was drawing letters on a chalkboard, which he came to see as forms.

He graduated from the university in Kumasi in 1968. In 1975 he began teaching at the University of Nigeria, Nsukka, and he was professor of sculpture there from 1996 to 2011. For years he worked mainly in wood and clay.

A bag by the road

The story of the bottle caps is often told, and not always the same way. Sculpture magazine says the first supply was a bag abandoned by the roadside. Ocula's account says the bag had been thrown out by a local distillery in Nigeria, and places the start of the work in the early 2000s. Wikipedia lists Man's Cloth, dated 1998 to 2001 and now in the British Museum, among the early pieces.

He began to experiment. Ocula describes the caps being cut, flattened, twisted, pierced and folded, then stitched together with copper wire.

Many hands

The scale needs a workshop. Sculpture magazine described teams of assistants, recruited near his studios in Nigeria and Ghana, who clip, flatten and link the caps into sheets. Tate speaks of dozens. Those sheets are modules. Ocula's account has Anatsui stepping in at the end to arrange them into the final composition.

He has said that the colours of the caps, the yellows, blacks and reds, led him to think like a painter as well as a sculptor.

After a retrospective organised by the curator Okwui Enwezor at the Haus der Kunst, Ocula reports, he moved back to Ghana and set up a large studio in Tema, outside Accra. Tate gives Tema and Nsukka as the places he lives and works.

Nothing is fixed

Because the sheets are flexible, the works have no single correct shape. They can be draped, bunched or stretched, and they are hung differently each time they are shown. Tate calls this a "non-fixed form". The people installing them make real decisions. That is unusual for sculpture, and deliberate.

The Turbine Hall

The largest test came in London. For Tate Modern's Hyundai Commission, Anatsui made Behind the Red Moon, shown in the Turbine Hall from October 2023 to April 2024. It came in three parts: The Red Moon, The World and The Wall.

Tate's guide describes thousands of bottle tops and metal fragments crumpled, crushed and joined by hand with copper wire. The first hanging, in red, formed the outline of a blood moon in eclipse and billowed like a sail.

Why bottle caps

The material is not neutral. Spirits were among the goods traded along the routes that carried enslaved people across the Atlantic, and Tate's guide ties the work to those histories of power and survival. In the same guide Anatsui recalls seeing the Tate & Lyle sugar name as a child in the Gold Coast, as Ghana then was. The caps are cheap, local and plentiful. They also carry a past.

That is the second life of the title. The object is saved from the roadside, and its history comes with it.

articles.title: Painting Without a Brush: Knives, Fingers and Chisels
articles.summary: A palette knife, a fingertip, a chisel. Three artists who gave up the brush, and what each one got in return.
articles.description: Three artists who put the brush down: Zara Muse with a palette knife, Amoako Boafo with his fingers and Vhils with a chisel. A note on tools and what they change.
articles.body:
The brush is such an ordinary part of painting that we rarely ask what it does. It holds paint, it draws a line, it softens an edge. It also puts fifteen centimetres of wood between the artist and the picture. Some artists decide they want that distance gone.

The knife

Zara Muse told Art Plugged that she works only with a palette knife and a spatula. A knife cannot draw a thin line or blend gently. It lays paint down in flat pieces with clear edges. A face built this way is made of planes, and the paint stands proud of the canvas. The limit is the point. It forces decisions.

The finger

Amoako Boafo went further and removed the tool altogether. According to Colección SOLO, he began painting with his fingers in 2017. Colección SOLO describes the faces and hands as whirls of brown and black oil, set against brightly coloured clothes and minimal backgrounds.

So in a Boafo portrait you can see exactly where the hand has been. The body is alive with swirls. Everything around it is still.

The chisel

The Portuguese artist Vhils, born Alexandre Farto in 1987, does not add anything at all. He takes away. Using chisels, mallets, picks and jackhammers, he cuts into the plaster of old walls until a portrait appears in the layers underneath.

He calls the approach Scratching the Surface. His own biography dates its first public showing to Lisbon in 2007 and its international debut to the Cans Festival in London in 2008. The faces are usually of ordinary, unnamed people, and the walls are ones a city has neglected.

His gallery traces the idea to the walls he grew up with outside Lisbon, thick with decades of posters and paint. To carve into them is to read the history of the place.

What the tool decides

Put the three side by side and a pattern shows. Each tool leaves a different kind of evidence. The knife leaves an edge. The finger leaves a touch. The chisel leaves a wound that becomes a face.

None of this makes the brush wrong. But a change of tool is never only technical. It changes how close the artist stands, how fast they can work and what kind of mistake is possible. The picture you end up looking at is, in part, a record of that choice.
