articles.title: Njideka Akunyili Crosby: Two Homes in One Picture
articles.summary: From across the room it is a quiet domestic scene. Up close, the walls and floors turn out to be made of hundreds of photographs.
articles.description: Njideka Akunyili Crosby layers paint, collage and photo transfer to picture a life between Nigeria and the United States. A reported profile.
articles.alt: Njideka Akunyili Crosby, with her hair pulled back, speaking in a plain white room during a filmed interview.
articles.credit: Njideka Akunyili Crosby interviewed by the Bronx Museum Teen Council, November 2014. A still from their film. Photo: Bronx Museum Teen Council, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.
articles.body:
A couple at a table. A woman on a sofa. A room with a patterned floor. Njideka Akunyili Crosby paints ordinary moments at home. Then you step closer and the surfaces dissolve into images: faces, magazine pages, family snapshots, printed into the picture itself.

Enugu to Los Angeles

She was born in Enugu, Nigeria, in 1983, one of six children. The Carnegie Corporation records that her father was a surgeon and her mother a professor of pharmacology who later served in the Nigerian government. As a girl she was sent to boarding school in Lagos.

At sixteen she moved to the United States, following her mother, who had won a place through the Diversity Visa lottery. The family expected her to study medicine. A painting class at a community college in Philadelphia changed her mind. She went on to Swarthmore College, where she studied biology and art and met her husband, Justin Crosby, then to the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts and to Yale, where she finished her MFA in 2011. After a residency at the Studio Museum in Harlem she settled in Los Angeles, where she lives and works.

How the pictures are built

Her works combine acrylic paint, charcoal, coloured pencil, fabric, collage and photo transfer. The transfers are made with acetone, which lifts a printed image and sets it down on the paper, slightly softened.

The source material is personal. She uses photographs she has taken in Nigeria, pictures from family albums and pages from popular Nigerian magazines. Laid side by side, they become wallpaper, clothing and floors inside the painted room.

Two worlds, one room

The Carnegie Corporation, which named her among its Great Immigrants in 2020, describes work that ranges from the legacy of colonialism in Africa to the experience of being an immigrant in America. Her own family is in it. Her parents, her siblings and her husband all appear, and one painting in The Beautyful Ones shows her older sister as a girl. She told the Carnegie Corporation that her home is "Nigeria and the United States at the same time".

What is striking is how gently it is done. Nothing is announced. Faces from magazines and albums sit in the pattern of a dress or a floor, and you find them only by looking closely. She has named Chinua Achebe as an influence, and told The Artist Profile Archive that a Nigerian looking at the work has "a whole other experience".

The effect is close to how memory works. The present scene is in front of you, and the past is in everything around it.

Recognition

In 2017 she received a MacArthur Fellowship, often called the genius grant. In 2018 the National Portrait Gallery in London showed her series The Beautyful Ones. She is represented by Victoria Miro and David Zwirner.

Why it matters

Many artists have pictured life between two countries as a kind of split. Akunyili Crosby pictures it as a layering. Both homes are present at once, in the same room, on the same sheet of paper. That is a more accurate account of how a great many people now live.

articles.title: Amoako Boafo and the Portrait Painted by Hand
articles.summary: He paints faces and hands with his own fingers. You can see the touch in every one of them.
articles.description: Amoako Boafo paints the skin of his sitters with his fingers. A reported profile of the Ghanaian artist, from Accra to Vienna and back.
articles.alt: Amoako Boafo in a white T-shirt, sitting on the edge of a white table in his studio, with large unfinished portraits of figures on pink and pale blue grounds on the walls behind him.
articles.credit: Amoako Boafo in his studio, July 2020. Photo: Francis Kokoroko, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.
articles.body:
Look closely at the skin in an Amoako Boafo portrait. It is made of swirls and ridges of oil paint, browns and blacks pushed around by a fingertip. The clothes are bright and the background is plain. All the movement is in the body.

Accra to Vienna

Boafo was born in Accra, Ghana, on 10 May 1984. Colección SOLO records that he taught himself to paint when young and supported himself for a time as a semi-professional tennis player. He graduated from the Ghanatta College of Art and Design in 2008 as its best portrait painter, and in 2014 moved to Austria to study at the Academy of Fine Arts in Vienna.

Vienna gave him two things. One was the example of Egon Schiele, whose twisting, expressive figures SOLO names as an inspiration. The other was harder. SOLO notes that he met racism and stereotyping there, and quotes him: "I want to be seen, not the stereotype." Wikipedia reports that he was once told his figures were "too black".

The fingers

According to Colección SOLO, it was in 2017 that he decided to start painting with his fingers. The faces and hands are formed by whirls of brown and black oil paint, while the clothes are brightly coloured and the backgrounds kept to a minimum.

The effect is that touch itself becomes part of the meaning. These are portraits of friends, family and people he admires, and the paint on their faces has been laid there by hand.

A fast rise

The art market noticed quickly. Ocula reports that in 2020 his painting The Lemon Bathing Suit, made the year before, sold at auction for £675,000. The same year he worked with Dior on its spring and summer 2021 menswear collection.

Museums followed. Soul of Black Folks opened at the Museum of the African Diaspora in San Francisco in 2021. Ocula records that it travelled to the Contemporary Arts Museum Houston in 2022 and the Seattle Art Museum in 2023, though other accounts list different stops. In 2024 the Belvedere in Vienna showed more than fifty works under the title Proper Love, hanging some beside Schiele and Klimt.

Home again

It would be easy to tell this as a story about prices. A better one is about place. Ocula reports that he lives between Accra and Vienna, and that in Accra he has opened dot.ateliers, in the Ogbojo district. The painter who left to study has gone back to build something.

articles.title: Amanza Smith Starts Again on Canvas
articles.summary: Television audiences know the name already. The paintings ask to be looked at without it.
articles.description: Amanza Smith, known from television, made her debut as a painter at MASH Gallery in Los Angeles. A reported profile of her mixed media work.
articles.body:
Amanza Smith came to painting with a public profile. She is known to television viewers from the property series Selling Sunset, and MASH Gallery in Los Angeles, which gave her a debut, lists her as a model, actress, interior design expert, luxury estate agent, DIY enthusiast and mental health advocate. The question any such artist faces is whether the work holds up once the name is covered.

Indiana

She grew up in Indiana, and the Majorca Daily Bulletin reported that there was not much money. She was a dancer and a gymnast before she was a painter.

A long stay in hospital

Painting came after a crisis. The same report says she began during a long stay in hospital, when she was given 24 to 48 hours to live and could use only her right arm.

A debut in Los Angeles

She was discovered through Instagram. The Bulletin reports that her first show was a group exhibition in Los Angeles with about fourteen artists, and that her first painting sold for US$18,000. MASH Gallery gave her a debut as an exhibiting artist.

What the paintings are made of

The work is mixed media on canvas. Gallery notes for Scattered Remnants and Circuit Riot describe robotic figures, circuitry, glitch effects and graffiti-like marks, with a nod to Basquiat. She calls the robots "botsquiats". Be Happy takes in pages of her own writing, headed On Being Happy.

How she works

She told the Bulletin that she never comes to a canvas with a subject in mind, and that she paints in a converted garage. She also said she expects some people to think she is not a real artist.

Some viewers will find the work too direct. But it is consistent. These are open-hearted pictures, more interested in energy than in irony.

To Europe

In April 2025 Grove Gallery showed her in London, with 404: Humanity not Found in Fitzrovia. The same month her work crossed to Mallorca, where Grove opened a space in Palma with Beyond The Surface, showing her alongside Zara Muse and Silent Mike.

A fair test

Fame gets an artist through the door quickly, and it also means many people decide what they think before they look. The fair test is the ordinary one. Stand in front of the canvas. See whether the colour, the layering and the marks keep your attention once you stop thinking about who made them.

articles.title: Robi Walters: Petals Cut from Broken Records
articles.summary: He cuts petals from broken vinyl and old packaging, and arranges them into flowers that seem to burst off the wall.
articles.description: Robi Walters builds lotus-like collages from broken vinyl records and discarded packaging. A reported profile of his practice, materials and daily routine.
articles.body:
Robi Walters was born in London in 1973 and still works there. His material is what other people throw away.

Rubbish, rearranged

The collages are made from discarded flyers, cardboard, household packaging and broken vinyl records. He cuts these into petal shapes, hundreds of them, and layers them outward from a centre. The Week compared the effect to fireworks, or to lotus flowers bursting open.

The lotus is not an accident. Cent Magazine traces it to his first sculpture, a cereal box cut into petals and arranged by sacred geometry into a thousand-petalled lotus. He has said that recycled card carries an energy that new material lacks.

A day with two ends

His routine has a shape. The artist Adelaide Damoah, writing in 2017, noted that he meditates every morning and ends each day with a painting, a kind of diary in paint. Cent Magazine reported where the habit came from: the Turner Prize winner Chris Ofili advised him to paint every day. The Week remembers the advice as to draw every day.

Since 2011 he has made a painting a day, each named after a news headline. In 2016 the Hospital Club in London showed them as 365: Every Day Counts.

So there are two bodies of work running side by side. The slow, exact collages, and the quick daily paintings that keep the hand moving.

Where it comes from

Walters has spoken openly about a difficult childhood. Cent Magazine reported that he was placed with a foster family at five, and The Week that he spent time in and out of children's homes because his mother was not able to cope. He told The Week that none of his art really makes sense unless you know his story. Today, Cent reports, he sees his mother every day and keeps in touch with his foster family.

In that light the choice of material reads less like a style and more like a statement: nothing is beyond being made into something.

Recognition

The Week reported in January 2018 that, at forty-four, he had just opened a gallery of his own on Ingestre Place in Soho. The same profile mentions small portraits inspired by African barber paintings, and a 2012 piece about Usain Bolt. In November 2023 Grove Gallery gave him a solo show, A Nation of Millions, in Fitzrovia, and in September 2024 it included him in its residency at South Place Hotel in east London.

Stand in front of one of the collages and you can still read fragments of the old life of the material: a groove, a scrap of lettering, the edge of a label. That is the point. The record is broken. It has become something else.

articles.title: Frank Canvas and the One-Line Joke
articles.summary: Some pictures need a wall text. A Frank Canvas needs only its title.
articles.description: Frank Canvas makes satirical limited edition prints with one-line titles. A short reported profile, drawn from his gallery's published material.
articles.body:
A note on sources first. Almost everything published about Frank Canvas comes from Grove Gallery, which represents and sells his work. We have found no independent interview or review. So this is a short profile, and it leans on the gallery's own description.

What the gallery says

Grove Gallery calls him an emerging artist who blends humour, satire and social commentary. Elsewhere it describes a bold, tongue-in-cheek approach to contemporary culture, with work meant to challenge, entertain and start conversations.

The titles do the talking

The clearest evidence is the list of titles. My Favourite Park. Choose Your Reality. Shopaholic. Karma. Coffee. Better Days. I Like Your Glasses. Each reads like the caption to a cartoon, or a message typed with one thumb. They point at the small rituals of modern life: shopping, caffeine, self-improvement, the phone.

This is satire at the scale of the everyday. The targets are not politicians or institutions. They are habits most of us recognise in ourselves.

Made to be owned

The format matters as much as the joke. The gallery sells them as signed limited editions. Choose Your Reality, for example, is an edition of 125, offered in sizes from A3 to A0. That is a deliberate choice. It keeps prices within reach of someone buying art for the first time, and it means the same image hangs in many homes.

There is a long line of artists who have worked this way, from the pop artists of the 1960s to the street artists whose prints sell out online in minutes. The edition is the artwork's natural form, not a souvenir of some larger original.

On the wall

Grove Gallery records his work in its rolling residency at South Place Hotel in east London, shown with Zen Xander and Robi Walters. A hotel suits this kind of picture. It is seen in passing, and it has a few seconds to make a stranger smile.

We would like to know more: where he trained, how the images are made, what he reads. When we can report that first-hand, we will.

articles.title: Zen Xander: One Name, Many Hands
articles.summary: A lion in a virtual reality headset eating salad. The joke lands at once. The harder question is who made it.
articles.description: Zen Xander is described as an anonymous street artist and, on the artist's own site, as a collective. A reported profile of the satirical work.
articles.body:
Most artist profiles begin with a person. This one cannot, because the accounts of who Zen Xander is do not agree.

Two versions

Society Falling opened at Grove Gallery in Fitzrovia in June 2024. Reviewing it in July, Art Plugged introduced Zen Xander as an anonymous street artist known for a satirical approach to fine art, moving from the street into the gallery. Artsy lists the show as a first solo exhibition, running from 26 June to 31 July 2024.

The artist's own website tells it differently. It says Zen Xander is not a single artist but a small group of painters, illustrators, designers and writers who share one aim: to make art that is warm, funny and easy to recognise yourself in.

We cannot settle which account is the fuller one, and we will not guess. It is worth noticing that both can be true of a name. A signature can belong to a studio as easily as to a hand.

The work

What is not in doubt is what the pictures look like. Animals are placed in human situations and left to carry the argument. Art Plugged described VR Vegan, in which a lion wears a virtual reality headset while eating a bowl of salad, as a jab at the gap between real and virtual life and at the contradictions of modern diets.

The humour is quick and visual. Another work in the show, Always a Cheetah, puts a cheetah on a scooter.

Why animals

Satire needs a little distance. Put a person in the picture and the viewer starts asking who it is meant to be. Put a cheetah or a cat there and everyone is free to see themselves. It is an old trick, as old as fables, and it suits an artist, or a group of artists, who would rather not be the story.

Out of the gallery

The work has not stayed in Fitzrovia. Grove Gallery's own record of its exhibitions lists Zen Xander pieces at South Place Hotel in east London, alongside Frank Canvas and Robi Walters, and a continuation of Society Falling at a Dorsett hotel in London.

An anonymous name, a recognisable style and a joke that reads in two seconds. Whoever holds the spray can, the formula is clear.

articles.title: Portraiture, Celebrity and Contemporary Cultural Memory
articles.summary: A portrait of a famous face is never only a likeness. It is a bid for how that person will be remembered.
articles.description: How contemporary portraiture turns public figures into cultural icons, from Warhol's Marilyn to Zara Muse's Malala and Konn Artiss's melting effigies.
articles.body:
In 1962, within weeks of Marilyn Monroe's death, Andy Warhol made the Marilyn Diptych. Fifty repeated faces, half in bright colour and half fading to grey. More than sixty years on, it is hard to picture Monroe without picturing Warhol's version of her.

That is the power of the celebrity portrait. It does not just record fame. It fixes a particular image of it in the shared memory.

Who gets painted now

For most of history the answer was simple: whoever could pay. Kings, merchants, their families. The portrait was proof of standing. Today artists more often choose their own subjects, and the choice is itself a statement about who deserves a place on the wall.

Zara Muse chose Malala Yousafzai. She told Art Plugged the subject stood for resilience, bravery and strength. The portrait sold at Bonhams in London in April 2025 for £51,200 including premium. Set aside the price and look at the decision. A painter known for portraits of women picked a living campaigner for girls' education and gave her the full weight of thick paint and saturated colour. That is an argument about who our icons should be.

When the famous are artists

Konn Artiss turned the same lens on the art world. For ANTI-FRIEZE in October 2025, the anonymous artist froze small effigies of Damien Hirst, Andy Warhol, Tracey Emin, Jeff Koons and KAWS in blocks of ice outside Frieze London and let them melt.

Art Plugged read the work as a comment on artistic immortality. It is also, in its odd way, a group portrait. These five are among the few artists famous enough to be recognised as dolls. The piece asks how long that kind of fame lasts once the conditions around it change.

Memory is a choice

Put the two beside each other and a pattern shows. One artist builds a face up in paint so that it will last. The other builds faces in ice so that they will not. Both are working on the same material, which is public memory.

A portrait of a living person is always a little early. The story is not finished and the painter is guessing at the ending. That is what makes the form risky, and why it still matters. When you next stand in front of a famous face in paint, ask who chose it, and what they are hoping you will remember.

articles.title: When Art Enters the World of Luxury Hospitality
articles.summary: Paintings are leaving the white room for the hotel bar. It is worth asking what they gain there, and what they give up.
articles.description: What happens when contemporary art moves into luxury hotels and restaurants, with Zara Muse at Fairmont Windsor Park as a case study in cultural partnerships.
articles.body:
A gallery asks for a certain kind of attention. You go on purpose, you stand, you look, you leave. A hotel asks for nothing. People sit for an hour with a drink and the painting is simply there, at the edge of the conversation.

A case in Windsor

In November 2024, FAD Magazine reported on a year-long partnership between Grove Gallery and the Fairmont Windsor Park hotel. Fourteen works from a new collection by Zara Muse were hung in the hotel's Bar 1215 and in its fine dining restaurant.

The launch was tied to a second partnership. Astrea London, which makes lab-grown diamonds, opened a boutique in the hotel, and Muse made a centrepiece portrait called Revolution that incorporates a 14.9 carat diamond.

It is not a one-off. Luxury News Online reported in March 2025 that her work also hangs in Kanishka, a restaurant in Mayfair, and that she had expanded into Dubai. Art Plugged described her paintings in hotel lobbies and private homes across Europe and the Middle East.

What the art gains

The first gain is time. A guest may spend longer near a painting in a bar than most visitors spend in front of anything in a museum. The second is audience. Many people who would never walk into a commercial gallery will happily spend an evening in a hotel.

FAD reported the gallery's view: that art should be accessible and part of everyday life, and that these rooms let it become part of the surroundings instead of a static display.

What it risks

The risk is the same thing seen from the other side. Art that becomes part of the surroundings can become furniture. Hotels choose work that suits a mood, and difficult or uncomfortable pictures rarely make the cut. A painting set beside a diamond is also, plainly, being asked to do a job for a brand.

Questions for the visitor

None of that is a reason to look away. It is a reason to look properly. Next time you find a painting in a hotel, ask three things. Is the artist named? Is there anything to tell you about the work? Could you see it without booking a table? The answers say a good deal about whether the art is a guest in the room or just part of the décor.

articles.title: Konn Artiss and the Relationship Between Object and Spectacle
articles.summary: A block of ice, a parody newspaper, a mannequin on a canal. Konn Artiss makes objects that are built to disappear, and events that are built to stay.
articles.description: Konn Artiss makes objects designed to vanish: melting ice, a parody newspaper, a floating mannequin. A reported essay on public interventions and spectacle.
articles.body:
On the morning visitors arrived at Frieze London in October 2025, five large blocks of ice were standing outside the main entrance. Art Plugged reported that each weighed 40 stone and each held a miniature effigy of a famous name: Damien Hirst, Andy Warhol, Tracey Emin, Jeff Koons and KAWS.

The work was called ANTI-FRIEZE. Then it melted. By the account in Art Plugged, what remained was puddles, bananas and a crowd caught between curiosity and discomfort.

An artist nobody has met

Konn Artiss is anonymous. The earliest reports we found date from June 2025. FAD Magazine reported a stunt in Washington DC built around The Washington Ghost, a parody newspaper aimed at Jeff Bezos shortly before his wedding in Venice. FAD noted that the name Konn Artiss had surfaced on social media with the sign-off "Trust Me".

The action then moved to Venice itself. GB News reported mannequins of Bezos and his fiancée floating along the Grand Canal in a gondola, and said more than 10,000 copies of the newspaper had been handed out.

The object

Look at what these works are made of. Frozen water. Newsprint. Shop mannequins. Fruit. None of it is meant to last, and none of it can be hung on a wall and sold in the usual way. The ice is the clearest case. It is a sculpture with a clock inside it.

The bananas are harder to read. It is difficult not to think of Maurizio Cattelan, who taped one to a wall at an art fair in 2019 and watched it become one of the most discussed artworks of the decade. That reading is ours, not the artist's.

The spectacle

If the object vanishes, where is the artwork? Mostly in what happens around it: the people who stop, the photographs they take, the reports that follow. Art Plugged read ANTI-FRIEZE as a comment on value, hype and decay, and on an art market that prizes permanence. The melting made that argument without a word of wall text.

This is the tension the work lives on. It mocks spectacle and depends on it completely. An intervention that nobody photographs has, in practical terms, not happened.

What is left

What stays behind is the record and the question. With an anonymous artist there is no biography to lean on, and with a melted sculpture there is no object to revisit. We are left to decide whether the event said something true. In October 2025, outside the tent where art is bought and sold, a lot of people stopped to watch famous names drip away. That is worth reporting.

articles.title: The Role of Personal Experience in Artistic Practice
articles.summary: A life does not explain a painting. But it often explains why the painting exists at all.
articles.description: How lived experience shapes artistic practice, from Zara Muse's return to painting to artists who withhold their biography altogether.
articles.body:
Ask an artist where the work comes from and the first answer is usually about materials or method. The second answer, if you wait for it, is usually about something that happened to them.

One account

Zara Muse has been open about hers. In an interview with Art Plugged in April 2025 she described caring for her mother through cancer, and her mother's death in February 2019. She said the loss changed her and made her more determined. She began painting again during the lockdown of 2020.

She has also spoken about what she left behind. Before painting she worked in finance and trading. She told the same interviewer that the old career does not feed directly into the pictures, but that leaving it gave her room to find herself. The portraits that followed are of women, and she describes them as a tribute to resilience.

None of this tells you whether a given portrait is good. What it tells you is what the artist was looking for when she picked up the knife.

A long tradition

She is in old company. Frida Kahlo began painting in earnest while confined to bed after a bus accident in 1925, and her own body remained her subject for the rest of her life. Louise Bourgeois returned to her childhood again and again across a career that lasted into her nineties. Tracey Emin showed her own unmade bed in 1998 and made the private life of the artist a public question.

The risk

There is a danger in all this. A moving story can be used to sell a weak picture, and a strong picture can be flattened into an illustration of its maker's biography. Viewers are right to be wary when the story arrives before the work does.

The opposite choice

Some artists refuse the bargain entirely. Konn Artiss, whose public interventions we report on in this issue, works anonymously. There is no childhood, no studio portrait and no origin story on offer. The work has to stand on what it does in the street.

Both approaches are honest in their way. One says: this is where it came from. The other says: that is none of your business, look at the thing. As readers and viewers, our job is the same in each case. Look first. Then, if the artist has offered it, listen to the story and see whether the work can carry it.

articles.title: Why Contemporary Artists Are Returning to Texture
articles.summary: Most of the art we see now arrives on glass. That may be exactly why surfaces that cast their own shadows feel so alive.
articles.description: Why thick paint, raw materials and visible handwork matter again in contemporary art. An essay on texture, impasto and the limits of the screen.
articles.body:
We should be honest at the start. There is no survey that proves painters are turning back to texture, and we will not pretend to have one. What we can report is what we see in the work we cover, and offer an argument for why it matters.

Thick paint is old

Texture is not a new idea. Rembrandt's late paintings are heavy with built-up paint. Van Gogh pushed pigment around until the strokes became the subject. In London, Frank Auerbach spent decades loading and scraping his canvases until the surface stood out like relief. Painters call the technique impasto, and it has never fully gone away.

What a screen cannot carry

What has changed is how we look. A phone shows every artwork at the same size, at the same brightness and with the same smooth finish. A photograph of a thickly painted canvas keeps the colour and loses almost everything else: the depth, the weight, the way a ridge of paint throws a small shadow as the light moves.

Texture is the part of a painting that does not survive that journey. For an artist, that makes it valuable. It is a reason to stand in front of the work itself, and it is proof that a hand was there.

Two examples from our pages

Zara Muse, whose portraits we look at elsewhere in this issue, told Art Plugged that she paints only with a palette knife and a spatula. Her surfaces are made of planes and edges, closer to modelling than to drawing. The material is doing some of the talking.

Konn Artiss works at the other extreme. For ANTI-FRIEZE in October 2025, the artist left five blocks of ice outside Frieze London, each holding a small figure of a famous artist. Ice is texture with a time limit. It was cold, wet and heavy, and then it was a puddle. Nobody who was there needed a caption to understand the material.

A caution

Texture is not meaning. Thick paint can be as empty as thin paint, and a rough surface can be a habit as easily as a decision. The question worth asking in front of any heavily worked piece is a simple one: what would be lost if this were smooth? When there is a real answer, the texture has earned its place.

articles.title: Zara Muse and the Physical Language of Portraiture
articles.summary: She paints with a palette knife and a spatula, and nothing else. The result is portraiture you read almost as much by its surface as by its likeness.
articles.description: Zara Muse paints portraits with a palette knife and a spatula. A reported essay on her artistic practice, her biography and what the knife does to a face.
articles.body:
People who write about Zara Muse tend to borrow their words from sculpture. Art Plugged, which interviewed her in April 2025, described thick layers, sculptural depth and saturated colour. That is not a flourish. It is a plain account of what happens when a painter puts down the brush.

What the knife does

Muse told Art Plugged that she works only with a palette knife and a spatula. The choice shapes everything that follows. A brush can draw a line and soften it. A knife lays paint down in flat planes, each with an edge and a thickness of its own. You cannot fuss with it. A cheekbone becomes a single loaded stroke, a shadow becomes a slab of darker colour set beside it.

So a face made this way is built more than it is drawn. Close up, it breaks into ridges and facets. Step back and the planes lock together into a person. The paint stands proud of the canvas and catches the light differently through the day, which is part of why these portraits hold their own in large rooms.

The person behind the name

Zara Muse is the working name of Alexandra Johnson. She has said the name gives her some privacy. Before painting she worked in finance and trading, a career she has described as intense and demanding. She later left that world and became a full-time carer for her mother, who was diagnosed with cancer in 2017 and died in February 2019.

According to the same interview, she began painting again during the 2020 lockdown, slowly at first and then with growing intensity. Her children and a cousin encouraged her to show the work in public. She is now represented by Grove Gallery in London.

Women, and what they carry

Her subject is women. Luxury News Online, which profiled her in March 2025, reported that she set out to paint women's faces and profiles across backgrounds and stages of life, with resilience as the thread running through them. She has also credited graffiti and street art with giving her a love of bold colour.

The best-known example is her portrait of Malala Yousafzai, a subject she chose for bravery and strength. Art Plugged reported that it sold at Bonhams in London on 3 April 2025 for £51,200 including premium. The same report lists earlier results at Tate Ward: £33,750 for In Her Own Light and £47,500 for The Shape of Stillness.

A language you can see being spoken

What makes this a physical language is that the surface keeps a record of its own making. Every stroke shows its direction and its pressure. Nothing is blended away. In a period when most images reach us flat and backlit, a portrait that so openly shows the work of a hand is saying something before the face has said anything at all.

artists.line: Our reporting on Banksy: the anonymous artist from Bristol, his stencil work, and how his work is authenticated.
artists.about:
An artist who works anonymously, first seen on walls and trains in Bristol in the 1990s. The work is authenticated by Pest Control, the artist's own office, and auction houses do not agree on a year of birth.

Bristol, 2009

In the summer of 2009 the artist took over Bristol Museum in his home city. The show, Banksy Versus Bristol Museum, had about 100 works, was free, and ran until 31 August. It had been planned in secret since the October before. Visitors found an ice-cream van and portable toilets set out like Stonehenge among the paintings.

Our reading: the joke was about who pays. A council that had spent money cleaning his work off walls was now hanging it.

artists.name: Yayoi Kusama
artists.line: Our reporting on Yayoi Kusama: the Infinity Nets, the dots and the mirror rooms.
artists.about:
Born in Matsumoto in 1929, she trained in Kyoto, spent fifteen years in New York and returned to Tokyo in 1973. The repeated mark of the Infinity Nets became the dots, the pumpkins and the mirror rooms. She died in August 2026, aged 97.

A painter first

Kusama said that her wish, from early on, was simply to be a painter. In New York in the 1960s she knew Donald Judd, Andy Warhol, Joseph Cornell and Claes Oldenburg, and painted net canvases up to 33 feet long. She painted so much that she began to feel ill.

Her first mirrored room, Kusama's Peep Show or Endless Love Show, dates from 1966. In 1977, back in Japan, she chose to live in a psychiatric hospital in Tokyo, and kept a studio where she painted from nine in the morning until six. She wrote novels and poems there too, and called her work her saviour.

In their own words

My wish was to be a painter one day.Yayoi Kusama, Tate film, 2012
I write novels and poems, and I also paint in the hospital. They are my saviours.Yayoi Kusama, quoted by Tate
I would stand up to them all with a single polka dot.Yayoi Kusama, quoted by Tate

artists.name: El Anatsui
artists.line: Our reporting on El Anatsui: the sculptor of bottle caps and copper wire, and his years in Nsukka.
artists.about:
A Ghanaian sculptor who taught for decades at the University of Nigeria, Nsukka. For more than two decades he has made vast, flexible hangings from liquor bottle caps joined with copper wire, hung differently each time they are shown.

Teacher, then sculptor of cloth

Anatsui trained in Kumasi from 1965 to 1968 and taught sculpture at Nsukka for more than four decades. Before the bottle caps came driftwood: Akua's Surviving Children, from 1996, is made of it. The bottle-cap hangings reached London in 2002, at the October Gallery, and the British Museum bought two of them.

He has said he has a hidden aim of waking up the artist in everybody, and that used things carry a charge from their past. His studio in Ghana is about 80 metres long, and he likes it quiet: no music while the work is made.

In their own words

When something has been used, there is a certain charge, a certain energy.El Anatsui, The Art Newspaper, 2023
Freedom is so very important, it can ameliorate so many things.El Anatsui, The Art Newspaper, 2023
I don’t want music in the studio.El Anatsui, Studio International, 2023

artists.name: Beatriz Milhazes
artists.line: Our reporting on Beatriz Milhazes: the Rio painter, her plastic-sheet method and her Brazilian sources.
artists.about:
A Rio de Janeiro painter of the 1980s Generation. She paints motifs on plastic sheets and transfers them to canvas, building crowded pictures of circles, bands and flowers.

From journalism to the studio

Milhazes studied journalism before she turned to painting at the Parque Lage school in Rio. She grew up under Brazil's military dictatorship, which lasted from 1964 to 1985. She worked out her transfer method in 1989, and her studio is next to Rio's botanical garden.

She calls herself an abstract geometric artist, and says she feels like a scientist in the studio. Peeling a single painted layer off its plastic sheet can take up to ten hours. In 2023 Turner Contemporary in Margate gave her first UK museum show in over 20 years.

In their own words

I feel like a scientist; it’s about experimenting and challenging myself.Beatriz Milhazes, Studio International, 2023
Colour is something you can never learn enough about.Beatriz Milhazes, Ocula, 2015
Yes, I’m shifting low art into high art.Beatriz Milhazes, Ocula, 2015

artists.name: S.H. Raza
artists.line: Our reporting on S.H. Raza: the Progressive Artists' Group, the French landscapes and the bindu.
artists.about:
An Indian painter and a founder of the Progressive Artists' Group in Bombay. He moved to Paris in 1950, painted the landscapes of France, and from 1980 built his work around the bindu. He returned to India late in life and died in New Delhi in 2016.

The forest and the dot

Raza was the son of a forest ranger. In 2001 he said his most lasting memory was the fear and fascination of the Indian forests. He went to Bombay in 1943, and in 1950 to Paris, where he met the gallerist Lara Vincy in 1955. In 1962 he taught at Berkeley.

He married the French artist Janine Mongillat, and went home to India after her death. Of the bindu, the dot at the centre of the late paintings, he said in 2010: it is the centre of my life. Ashok Vajpeyi has passed on another of his lines: how he painted he learned from France, what he painted came from India.

In their own words

The most tenacious memory of my childhood is the fear and fascination of Indian forests.S.H. Raza, 2001, quoted by Christie's
Rothko’s work opened up lots of interesting associations for me.S.H. Raza, quoted by Christie's

artists.name: Gerhard Richter
artists.line: Our reporting on Gerhard Richter: the photo paintings, the squeegee abstracts and the move west.
artists.about:
A German painter who left Dresden for the West in 1961. He has worked for decades in two strands at once: blurred paintings made from photographs, and abstracts dragged across the canvas with a squeegee.

Leaving at 29

Richter was 29 when he left East Germany in 1961 to study in Düsseldorf. More than half a century later he made Birkenau (2014), working from four photographs smuggled out of the death camp in 1944. Photographs record the paintings in progress over six weeks that summer.

He has said that helplessness is the great theme of painting, and that it is not unusual for him to start with a figure and end with an abstract. The Met's 2020 show, Painting After All, put more than 100 works together, from 1962 to 2020.

In their own words

Helplessness is the great theme in painting, or rather the strongest motivation for and during painting.Gerhard Richter, 2014, quoted by the Met
Art requires freedom … in dictatorships there is no art, not even bad art.Gerhard Richter, quoted by the Met

artists.name: OSGEMEOS
artists.line: Our reporting on OSGEMEOS, the twin brothers from São Paulo: graffiti, murals and the world they paint.
artists.about:
Gustavo and Otavio Pandolfo, twin brothers born in 1974, who began in graffiti and work as one. Their long-limbed yellow figures appear on walls, a Scottish castle and gallery canvases.

Two people, one artist

The twins grew up in Cambuci, a working-class part of São Paulo. As children they made up a world of their own, which they call Tritrez, and the yellow of their figures is said to be a colour both of them see in dreams. Their teenage notebooks were shown for the first time at the Pinacoteca de São Paulo in 2020.

They describe themselves as one artist. Otavio has said the two of them talk in a way only they can hear. In 2024 the Hirshhorn in Washington opened Endless Story, their first major museum survey in the United States.

In their own words

We are like one artist.Gustavo Pandolfo, NPR, 2024
There is a conversation in the air flying there, but only we can listen [to] each other.Otavio Pandolfo, NPR, 2024

artists.name: Vhils
artists.line: Our reporting on Vhils, Alexandre Farto: carved walls, street posters and a method built on removal.
artists.about:
Alexandre Farto, who grew up in Seixal on the edge of Lisbon and started writing graffiti at thirteen. He makes portraits by taking material away: carving plaster, cutting posters and etching metal.

Destroying to reveal

At 16 or 17 Vhils began to question the graffiti he had been writing since 13. He tried painting billboards white and carving back into them, and found that taking away showed what was underneath. He calls himself a kind of urban archaeologist.

He went to London to study at about 19. His studio now sits in Barreiro, outside Lisbon, with a team of about 15. In Rio he worked with an NGO on houses in a favela that was being torn down. He has said he tries to give dignity to places that were left behind.

In their own words

I felt that by destroying I was revealing.Vhils, designboom, 2017
All of the layers in my work were a part of someone’s life before.Vhils, Hypebeast, 2020
I say that I’m kind of an urban archaeologist because I basically carve on the walls of the city.Vhils, Euronews

artists.name: KAWS
artists.line: Our reporting on KAWS, Brian Donnelly: graffiti, cartoons, COMPANION and sculpture.
artists.about:
Brian Donnelly, born in 1974, who painted backgrounds for television cartoons and repainted bus shelter adverts before making COMPANION, the figure with crossed-out eyes, in 1999.

From bus shelters to Victoria Harbour

KAWS made his first New York museum show, WHAT PARTY, at the Brooklyn Museum in 2021. In an interview that year he said he wants people to look at the form of his figures, not guess at what they might say. He has also said that, whatever he puts on canvas, people do not think of him as a painter.

The figures have grown huge: an inflatable about 121 feet long in Hong Kong's Victoria Harbour in 2019, and a hot air balloon of about 140 feet over Bristol in 2021. He has worked with Nike, Uniqlo and Dior.

In their own words

I want you to look at the form. I don’t want you to think about what they might say.KAWS, The Brooklyn Rail, 2021
When I make new works I’m thinking of it as adding a family member into this sort of dialogue with everything.KAWS, The Brooklyn Rail, 2021

artists.name: Eko Nugroho
artists.line: Our reporting on Eko Nugroho: Yogyakarta, masked figures, embroidery and community work.
artists.about:
An artist from Yogyakarta who works in painting, embroidery and sculpture, often with communities. His masked figures come from comics.

A teacher, a zine and a studio of 30

Nugroho was 20 when Suharto fell in 1998. He studied at the Indonesian Institute of the Arts in Yogyakarta, once worked as a primary school teacher, and in June 2000 started a comic zine, Daging Tumbuh. His first solo show, Bercerobong, was at Cemeti Art House in 2002.

He now runs a studio of about 30 people and an art class with about 50 students. In 2013 he showed in Indonesia's pavilion at Venice. The masks on his figures are deliberate: he has said he does not want to pass judgement on anyone.

In their own words

I don’t want to pass judgment on somebody. Such cases can happen to anybody in the future.Eko Nugroho on the masks, The Jakarta Post, 2017
I must understand the overall situation of the place where the mural will be.Eko Nugroho, quoted in Art + Australia

artists.name: Faith XLVII
artists.line: Our reporting on Faith XLVII: South African graffiti, murals in 39 countries and work beyond the wall.
artists.about:
A South African artist who began writing graffiti as Faith47 in 1997 and has since painted murals in 39 countries. Her work now includes tapestries, bronzes, paintings and prints.

From Clovelly station to the world

Faith XLVII was born in Cape Town. Her first wall was at the old Clovelly train station, painted with the writer Wealz130, and by the early 2000s she was one of the busiest names in South African graffiti. By 2020 she had been living in Los Angeles for three years.

She has said her works are not made to be pretty, but to make people think and question. She paints animals often: a zebra in Johannesburg, horses in Los Angeles, swans on a Brooklyn roof. And she accepts that walls do not last.

In their own words

These are not works made to be pretty or decorative; these are works made to consider, to dismantle, to question.Faith XLVII, Daily Maverick, 2020
We are not islands.Faith XLVII, Daily Maverick, 2020
One can’t stop the clouds from moving. Nothing is permanent.Faith XLVII, Brooklyn Street Art, 2018

artists.name: Vincent van Gogh
artists.line: Our reporting on Vincent van Gogh: the last weeks at Auvers, the chestnut trees and the long lives of his paintings after him.
artists.about:
Van Gogh was born in Zundert, in the south of the Netherlands, in 1853. In just over ten years of painting he made about 2,100 works and had little success while he lived. In May 1890 he left the asylum at Saint-Rémy for Auvers-sur-Oise, north of Paris. He painted about 70 pictures there in roughly as many days, and died in the village on 29 July 1890.

The last letters

His letters to his brother Theo show a painter thinking hard about what each picture should do. In July 1890 he wrote of new canvases of wide fields under troubled skies, made to express sadness and loneliness, and yet, he said, also how healthy the countryside made him feel. Six days before he died he sent Theo a sketch of Daubigny's garden and called it one of his most carefully thought-out canvases.

In their own words

I’m fairly sure that these canvases will tell you what I cannot say in words, that is, how healthy and invigorating I find the countryside.Vincent van Gogh to Theo and Jo, July 1890
Perhaps you will take a look at this sketch of Daubigny’s garden - it is one of my most carefully thought-out canvases.Vincent van Gogh to Theo, 23 July 1890

artists.name: Wassily Kandinsky
artists.line: Our reporting on Wassily Kandinsky: the move to abstraction, the Bauhaus years and the Guggenheim connection.
artists.about:
Kandinsky was born in Moscow in 1866 and studied law and economics. At 30 he gave up law for art and moved to Munich. In 1911 he founded the Blue Rider with Franz Marc, and in 1912 published On the Spiritual in Art. He returned to Germany in 1921 and joined the Bauhaus, then moved to France when the school closed under Nazi pressure in 1933. He died there in 1944.

A writer as well as a painter

He wrote as well as painted: Klänge (1913), with 56 woodcuts, and Point and Line to Plane (1926). Between 1909 and 1914 he wrote four stage works built on colour and sound, among them The Yellow Sound. None was produced while he lived.

In their own words

Every work of art is the child of its age and, in many cases, the mother of our emotions.Wassily Kandinsky, On the Spiritual in Art, translated by Michael Sadler

artists.name: Rene Matić
artists.line: Our reporting on Rene Matić: photographs of family, friends and community, the Turner Prize shortlist and the Deutsche Börse prize.
artists.about:
A London photographer, born in Peterborough in 1997, whose pictures of the people closest to them are shown with sound, flags and banners. Shortlisted for the Turner Prize 2025; winner of the Deutsche Börse Photography Foundation Prize 2026.

The work so far

Matić is an artist and writer who works in photography, film and sculpture. The solo shows have come quickly: Arcadia Missa in 2021, Studio Voltaire and the South London Gallery in 2022, the Martin Parr Foundation in 2023, and JAZZ, made with Oscar Murillo, at Kunsthalle Wien in 2024. The work is now in the collections of Tate, the Fondation Louis Vuitton and the Government Art Collection.

We have not yet found an interview we could quote with confidence, so this page gives the record rather than the artist's own words.

artists.name: Raven Halfmoon
artists.line: Our reporting on Raven Halfmoon: coil-built stoneware figures, Caddo history and a show that toured five venues.
artists.about:
A ceramic sculptor and citizen of the Caddo Nation, born in Norman, Oklahoma, in 1991. She builds stoneware figures by coiling clay, some more than 12 feet tall.

Clay by hand

Halfmoon is Caddo, and also has Choctaw, Delaware and Otoe heritage. At 13 she met the Caddo potter Jeri Redcorn, and went on to study anthropology and studio art at the University of Arkansas. She has said she went through about 8,000 pounds of clay with her hands, and that a firing can take two to three weeks.

She wants the making to show in the finished work, and calls galleries and museums her churches. She now works in bronze and stone as well: The Guardians (2024) is a bronze nine feet tall.

In their own words

Clay is my most intimate relationship.Raven Halfmoon, Southwest Contemporary, 2023
Galleries and museums are my churches.Raven Halfmoon, The Creative Independent, 2024
Art is our cultural preservation, it’s how we talk about what’s happening.Raven Halfmoon, The Creative Independent, 2024

artists.name: Dana Awartani
artists.line: Our reporting on Dana Awartani: traditional crafts, loss and repair, and Venice in 2024 and 2026.
artists.about:
A Palestinian-Saudi artist, born in Jeddah in 1987, who uses embroidery, natural dyes and geometry. She represented Saudi Arabia at the 2026 Venice Biennale.

Craft as a kind of prayer

Awartani studied at Central Saint Martins and then at the Prince's School of Traditional Arts in London. Her textiles are dyed with natural dyes by craftspeople in Trivandrum, India, and she commissions embroidery from Syrian women living as refugees in Jordan.

She does not make copies of her work. A recent sand piece grew out of Jeddah's old district, Al-Balad, and takes its title from the poet Mahmoud Darwish.

In their own words

Some people see craft as a form of prayer.Dana Awartani, Berlin Art Link, 2025
Nothing is mass-produced and I don’t make duplicates.Dana Awartani, Berlin Art Link, 2025

artists.name: Ana Segovia
artists.line: Our reporting on Ana Segovia: Mexican cowboy imagery, golden-age cinema and a fast-moving career.
artists.about:
A painter born in Mexico City in 1991, who reworks images from Mexican cowboy culture and film. Represented by kurimanzutto since 2023.

Pausing the film

Segovia's paintings start from film stills, many from the golden age of Mexican cinema and from Westerns. The artist has joked about being the worst person to watch a film with, pausing every few seconds. Three things guide the work: humour, eros and aggression.

At the 2024 Venice Biennale Segovia showed a first film, about two charros, with suits made by the grandson of Jorge Negrete's tailor. The 2025 series Ramón follows one invented man, whom Segovia has called a fantasy of who the artist wants to be.

Heroes are always these tough guys.Ana Segovia, Galerie, 2025
I’m always thinking about three things in art that are important to my process: humor, eros, and aggression.Ana Segovia, AnOther, 2025

artists.name: Jes Fan
artists.line: Our reporting on Jes Fan: glass, resin and biological materials, from Venice to a museum survey at Yale.
artists.about:
A sculptor born in Toronto in 1990 and raised in Hong Kong, who trained in glass and works with resin and materials such as melanin and testosterone.

Questions, not technique

Fan studied glass at the Rhode Island School of Design, but has said the interest is in process rather than technique. On a residency in 2018 Fan worked with melanin produced by E. coli bacteria. Since 2020 Fan has worked with agarwood, and used 3D scans of the artist's own body, for Sites of Wounding, shown in the Sigg Prize exhibition at M+ in 2023.

For Fan, art and science are both ways of asking questions, and craft was once a technology in its own right.

In their own words

Art and sciences are essentially just ways of questioning. They are not opposing in my world.Jes Fan, M+, 2023
I’m not interested in technique, I’m interested in process.Jes Fan, Wallpaper*, 2022
Craft used to be technological; back in the day, the loom was the first computer.Jes Fan, Wallpaper*, 2022

artists.name: Mohamed L'Ghacham
artists.line: Our reporting on Mohamed L'Ghacham: family photographs painted as murals, from Mallorca to Vienna.
artists.about:
A painter and muralist born in Tangier, Morocco, in 1993 and based in Mataró, near Barcelona. He paints old family and archive photographs across whole walls.

Painting what is real

L'Ghacham's parents moved from Tangier to Spain a few months after he was born, and he grew up in Mataró. He started painting in the street in 2008, as factories closed after the financial crisis. His first murals went on abandoned or half-demolished buildings and on the edges of towns. Juxtapoz reported in about 2022 that he had moved to Madrid.

He avoids posed scenes and looks for moments of calm and reunion. Murals are a race against the clock, he says, and if he were not a painter he would probably make films.

In their own words

I almost never depict acted scenes with people posing, I am keen on conveying what is authentic.Mohamed L'Ghacham, Street Art United States, 2017
My paintings usually represent moments of calm and reunion.Mohamed L'Ghacham, Juxtapoz
